pool.q: What postoperative complications can occur with laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), but do not occur with corneal implanted devices such as intrastromal corneal ring segments (ICRSs)?
pool.rationale: Irregular astigmatism and infectious keratitis can occur after both LASIK and intrastromal corneal ring segment implantation. Implant extrusion would only occur after segment implantation. Ectasia is a complication of LASIK, and intrastromal corneal ring segments are one potential treatment for ectasia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In the setting of refractive surgery, what are the typical consequences of significant higher-order aberrations?

options.a: symptoms of higher-order aberrations can be improved with spectacles
options.b: symptoms of higher-order aberrations are improved with dilation
options.c: symptoms of higher-order aberrations include glare, halos, or ghosting
options.d: symptoms of higher order aberrations are improved with LASIK surgery

pool.rationale: Patients with higher-order aberrations usually notice glare, halos, or ghosting. Lower-order aberrations (ie, spherocylindrical aberrations) can be treated with glasses or contact lenses and include myopia, hyperopia, and astigmatism. The symptoms are more apparent with dilation of the pupil. Higher-order aberrations cannot be treated with glasses, but contact lenses can reduce these aberrations. Coma, trefoil, and spherical aberration are examples of higher-order aberrations. Both lower- and higher-order aberrations can be treated with the excimer laser. Lower-order aberrations typically make up 90% of a patient's overall aberration profile while higher-order aberrations make up the remaining 10%. Several studies have shown that mechanical microkeratomes worsen higher-order aberrations while the femtosecond laser does not worsen them. In any event, LASIK flap creation does not improve higher-order aberrations.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 45-year-old hyperope desires monovision correction with contact lenses. The nondominant right eye is chosen for near work. The distance refraction (manifest and cycloplegic) is +2.00 sphere in the right eye. What contact lens power would be the most appropriate?
pool.rationale: Monovision in contact lenses, where one eye is corrected for distance and the other eye is corrected for an age-appropriate near correction, is often quite successful for patients to allow vision at a broader range of distances than would be possible with distance-only correction. At age 50, an additional +1.5 D of near power would be appropriate for most visual needs; thus, the use of a +3.5 D contact lens for a patient with a +2.00 D refractive error would be useful. A +5.0 D correction that would lead to approximately +3.0 D of near power would likely be more correction than needed, and the extra anisometropia could be more poorly tolerated. The levels of correction listed in the other answers would not allow adequate near vision.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: After creating the flap, the ophthalmologist notices that there is no hinge, and a free cap has been created, although the stromal bed is large enough for treatment. What is the best way to manage this complication?

options.a: Abort the laser treatment, dispose of the cap, and place a bandage contact lens.
options.b: Continue with laser treatment, dispose of the cap, place a bandage contact lens.
options.c: Place the cap in a moist chamber, continue with laser treatment, replace the cap, place a bandage contact lens.
options.d: Abort the laser treatment, hydrate the cap in sterile water to prevent striae, replace the cap, and place a bandage contact lens.

pool.rationale: After creating a free cap, the corneal cap should be placed in a moist chamber, not in sterile water. If the bed can accommodate the treatment, the laser ablation can be performed. The cap should be replaced and secured with a bandage contact lens. One can consider adding a suture as an artificial hinge.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What advantage does the femtosecond laser have compared to a mechanical microkeratome?

options.b: less incidence of diffuse lamellar keratitis
options.d: better control of the construction of the flap

pool.rationale: The femtosecond laser has several advantages over the mechanical microkeratome but the only one offered is that it provides better control over the construction of the flap. Variables such as flap location, diameter, thickness, and hinge location are able to be fine-tuned with the femtosecond laser. The frequency of other flap complications such as a free cap or buttonhole flap are reduced or eliminated. The femtosecond laser has not been shown to reduce the incidence of bacterial keratitis or diffuse lamellar keratitis and has not been shown to produce better visual acuity.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common adverse effect resulting from dry eyes after LASIK?
pool.rationale: Dry-eye symptoms are the most common adverse effects of refractive surgery and occasionally persist for months or years; they have been reported in 60%–70% of all patients, to varying degrees. Corneal sensitivity decreases after LASIK because of the surgical amputation of nerves during flap formation and the destruction of superficial nerve fibers during the laser ablation. This can result in corneal anesthesia lasting 3–6 months. As a result, most patients experience a decrease in tear production. Patients who had dry eyes before surgery or whose eyes were marginally compensated before surgery might have more severe symptoms. In addition, patients with dry eyes following LASIK or surface ablation have an abnormal tear film and a poor ocular surface and they often note fluctuating vision between blinks and at different times of the day.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How should microstriae in a patient with excellent vision on the first day after laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) be treated?

options.c: flap suturing with sutures oriented 90 degrees to the direction of the microstriae

pool.rationale:
Microstriae are fine, hairlike optical irregularities corresponding to fine folds in the Bowman layer, which can be seen on retroillumination. Management of microstriae depends on whether they affect visual acuity. If they do not affect vision, they can be observed. If they are visually significant, both suturing the flap and phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) are potential options for treatment.
Flap floating with and without hypertonic saline are options to treat visually significant macrostriae.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How is the risk of retinal detachment changed by laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), or radial keratotomy?

options.a: Retinal detachment risk is higher after LASIK and PRK and unaffected by radial keratotomy.
options.b: Retinal detachment risk is increased after all of these refractive procedures.
options.c: Retinal detachment risk is unaffected after any of these refractive procedures.
options.d: Retinal detachment risk is decreased after all of these refractive procedures.

pool.rationale:
Patients with high myopia should be counseled that refractive surgery corrects only the refractive aspect of the myopia and not the natural history of the highly myopic eye, with its known complications. Highly myopic patients remain at risk for retinal tears and detachment throughout their lives, despite refractive surgery. No causal link has been established between retinal detachment and excimer laser refractive surgery. Current data (albeit not well-controlled, long-term studies) suggest that surface ablation, radial keratotomy, and LASIK do not appear to increase the incidence of retinal detachment. Symptomatic retinal tears or subclinical retinal detachments should always be treated. Tears or holes associated with high myopia should be considered for treatment.
Retinal detachment repair may interfere with a previous LASIK flap; if corneal scraping during surgery is required, the flap may be disrupted, and the retinal surgeon should be made aware of prior LASIK before retinal detachment repair is undertaken.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with small palpebral fissures and tight eyelids, suction is lost during the microkeratome pass, resulting in the complication seen in the photo. How should the refractive treatment be completed?

options.a: Replace the flap, perform the ablation on top of the flap.
options.b: Replace the flap, recut at a deeper level, perform the ablation.
options.c: Replace the flap, perform the ablation after a few months.
options.d: Perform the ablation, replace the flap.

pool.rationale: Significant visual loss can occur if the ablation is performed after creation of a buttonhole flap. Waiting several months allows proper healing, after which either a new flap can potentially be produced at a deeper level, or surface ablation can be performed. Not waiting for healing can lead to the loss of the previously created flap.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 45-year-old myope desires monovision correction with laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). The nondominant right eye is chosen for near vision and has a refraction of -5.00 sphere. Assuming no nomogram adjustment is required, how many diopters of refractive treatment should be programmed into the laser?
pool.rationale: Monovision to modify presbyopia in phakic individuals can be an effective strategy to achieve reduced dependence on spectacles. The process involves intentionally undercorrecting a myopic patient, overcorrecting a hyperopic patient, or inducing mild myopia in an emmetrope. Many refractive surgeons target mild myopia after treatment (-0.50 to -1.50 D) to achieve good uncorrected near- to intermediate-distance vision, making a treatment of -3.50 D (leaving a residual of -1.50 D) the correct answer choice. Modified monovision would entail correction to achieve the lower end of myopia for the near-vision eye, and results in only a mild decrease in distance vision, retention of good stereopsis, and a significant increase in intermediate zone function.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 32-year-old woman who underwent bilateral laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) is noted to have the clinical findings shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The image shows typical epithelial ingrowth after LASIK. If the epithelium approaches the visual axis, causes decreased vision from irregular astigmatism, or triggers flap melting, then the flap should be lifted and the epithelium should be scraped from the undersurface of the flap and the corneal stroma.
Interface debris would have the appearance of foreign material under the flap. Early DLK would have a granular appearance under the flap, and infectious keratitis would typically present as a white opacity either on the corneal surface or under the flap.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During microkeratome flap construction in a laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) procedure, a patient's flap is noted to be irregular and decentered. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Replace the flap, do not complete the ablation, and suture the flap in place.
options.b: Complete the laser ablation and replace the flap.
options.c: Complete the laser ablation while protecting the hinge and replace the flap.
options.d: Replace the flap, do not complete the ablation, wait for complete healing and reassess refractive options.

pool.rationale: If the flap creation is suboptimal either from decentration, a buttonhole, or an irregular flap, the safest way to manage this problem is to replace the flap, wait for it to heal, and then reassess refractive options. A suture is usually not required to maintain a secure flap position. Performing a laser ablation can lead to irregular astigmatism.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the minimal thickness recommended for the residual stromal bed (RSB) following laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?
pool.rationale:
The strength of the cornea after laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) is greatly dependent on the residual stromal bed (RSB). RSB is calculated by taking the central corneal thickness and subtracting the presumed flap thickness and ablation depth. The ablation depth is determined by the patient’s actual refraction and non-nomogram-adjusted number used by physicians using the VISX laser. A RSB of at least 250 µm is recommended to avoid potential postoperative weakness in the cornea that may manifest as corneal ectasia.
Some surgeons are even more conservative and use 275 µm or 300 µm as their minimum stromal bed thickness. Some surgeons also use 500 µm as their minimum preoperative corneal thickness to reduce the risk of postoperative corneal ectasia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 28-year-old woman undergoes LASIK for myopic astigmatism with great success, achieving uncorrected distance vision of 20/20 one week after LASIK. She returns 3 years later, reporting blurring of her distance vision. She is noted to have uncorrected distance vision of 20/50 in her right eye and 20/60 in the left, with a refractive error of –1.25 +0.75 × 89 in the right eye and –1.00 +1.25 × 100 in the left eye. What is the best option for this patient?

options.a: Perform surface ablation to treat the refractive error.
options.b: Rule out cataract formation because nuclear cataracts can result in a myopic shift.
options.c: Assess the corneal topographic change and rule out post-LASIK ectasia.
options.d: Proceed with flap lift and touchup to treat the regression of her initial LASIK treatment.

pool.rationale: A post-LASIK myopic shift, especially with onset of with-the-rule astigmatism, can be a sign of post-LASIK ectasia. This patient’s corneas should be evaluated for ectatic changes using topographic imaging. If ectasia is noted, further ablative treatments should be avoided because they could lead to further decompensation of the corneal integrity. The patient should then be evaluated on an ongoing basis and considered for treatment and management of the ectasia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Larger optical zones and treatment areas reduce what complication of hyperopic refractive surgery?
pool.rationale:
Glare is a possible complication of both hyperopic and myopic excimer laser photoablation and can result from an abrupt transition between the optical zone and the untreated cornea. Because the sculpting to create a steeper central cornea in hyperopic treatments occurs with ablation of the midperipheral cornea, it is important to plan for, and program into the laser, an appropriate blend zone in hyperopic treatments to minimize an abrupt transition (figure). A prolate blend zone reduces glare and haloes following excimer laser photo ablation.
Regression of effect and residual refractive error can occur no matter what preoperative considerations and measures are employed. Use of nomograms is the primary manner in which final residual refractive error is adjusted, not through changing the optical zone. In general, patients with higher degrees of myopia and any degree of hyperopia require more time to attain refractive stability, which must be achieved prior to considering retreatment.
Postoperative discomfort can be managed effectively with oral analgesics and steroidal and nonsteroidal topical drops, as well as bandage contact lenses after surface ablations. Intraoperatively, chilled balanced salt solution (BSS) can be used to decrease postoperative discomfort. No effective preoperative method has been found to prevent discomfort postoperatively.
A larger optical zone and therefore more tissue ablation would increase the risk of postoperative ectasia. Ectasia is typically higher risk in LASIK, and in patients with thin corneas or higher myopic corrections or who have undergone several laser ablations. However, cases of ectasia without any demonstrable risk factors have also been reported.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What concentration of mitomycin C is appropriate for use in the prevention of photorefractive keratectomy-induced corneal scarring?
pool.rationale: The dosage of mitomycin C most commonly reported in the literature is 0.2 mg/mL (0.02%). There have been some reports of lower concentrations, but not higher concentrations than this strength. Therefore, concentrations of 200 mg/mL, 20 mg/mL, or 2 mg/mL have not been studied well enough to suggest usage.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with a history of eczema of her upper extremities presents for laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) evaluation.  She has been diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus but has no retinopathy on examination. She is a swim instructor and spends approximately 6 hours a day in chlorinated swimming pools. What in her history or examination may be a relative contraindication to having LASIK?
pool.rationale: A list of relative contraindications for excimer laser photoablation is shown in Figure 1. Pregnancy causes changes in refractive error and is therefore a relative contraindication for refractive surgical procedures. Swimming has not been shown to affect long-term refractive stability or results with refractive surgery. Eczema is also not a contraindication to refractive surgery as compared to connective tissue disease. Diabetic retinopathy is a relative contraindication to excimer laser photoablation, but simply having diabetes is not.

pool.q: Immediately following cataract surgery with a diffractive multifocal intraocular lens (IOL), a patient complains of visually disabling glare and halos that persist over the next several months. What is the best next step in management?

options.b: Nd:YAG capsulotomy, and if that fails, then an IOL exchange
options.c: IOL exchange with a monofocal IOL
options.d: IOL exchange with a refractive multifocal IOL

pool.rationale:
All multifocal lenses have the potential of causing halos. Many patients may experience fewer halos over several months, potentially from neural adaptation. However, should halos be disabling and persistent, a lens exchange may be the only option. A piggyback IOL would not address the halos.

While patients with multifocal IOLs may be more sensitive to posterior capsule opacification (PCO), symptoms from PCO are typically not present initially but gradually worsen over the first few weeks to months after surgery. In contrast, intrinsic IOL symptoms appear early, if not immediately, in the postoperative course and stay consistent over time. Additionally, performing a capsulotomy would make future lens exchanges more difficult.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 42-year-old man develops diffuse lamellar keratitis following bilateral myopic laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). He is treated with long-term frequent topical steroids and then develops a thin pocket of fluid in the lamellar interface. What is the relationship between this patient's measured applanation tonometry and true intraocular pressure (IOP)?

options.a: IOP measurements are not predictably related to actual IOP.
options.b: IOP measurements will accurately reflect actual IOP.
options.c: IOP measurements will be higher than actual IOP.
options.d: IOP measurements will be lower than actual IOP.

pool.rationale: This patient has pressure-induced stromal keratitis (PISK), which is characterized by a late-onset interface opacification often accompanied by an interface fluid cleft caused by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) after LASIK. PISK is often associated with prolonged corticosteroid treatment and resultant steroid response. Applanation tonometry can be measured at a value falsely lower than actual IOP, due to the fluid in the interface; therefore, it is important to measure IOP both centrally and peripherally using a tonopen or pneumotonometer. The other answer choices are incorrect because they do not describe the relationship accurately in this condition.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Two days after uneventful photorefractive keratectomy, a 25-year-old man with myopia has pain in his right eye. After removing his bandage contact lens, the ophthalmologist finds a 1.5-mm anterior stromal opacity and a 3-mm central epithelial defect. There is no anterior chamber reaction. What is the next step in management?

options.a: Add empiric coverage for fungal infections, since the patient is on topical corticosteroids.
options.b: Add more antibiotics to cover for gram-positive organisms, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
options.c: Return to the operating room for thorough irrigation of the corneal surface.

pool.rationale: This patient is presenting with infectious keratitis after refractive surgery. Because a large epithelial defect is created during the procedure, patients are at an increased risk for infection. The first step in management is to culture the infiltrate (and the bandage contact lens, if possible), making sure to culture for fungus as well as bacteria. While gram-positive organisms are most common and these patients are at increased risk for fungal infections, the first step in management must be to obtain cultures. There is no role for irrigating the corneal surface.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 45-year-old patient with myopia desires monovision correction with LASIK. The nondominant eye is chosen for near vision and has a refraction of –5.00 sphere. Assuming no nomogram adjustment is required, what is the most appropriate laser treatment setting?
pool.rationale: To create monovision in a myopic patient, it is necessary to undercorrect 1 eye, usually the nondominant eye. The amount of desired undercorrection is determined by a combination of the patient's requirements for near vision and the amount of anisometropia that is tolerable. In a 45-year-old patient, 1.50 D is generally the appropriate amount of undercorrection for providing functional near vision without generating significant problems with anisometropia if the nondominant eye requires correction with glasses for activities such as driving at night. This refraction allows good uncorrected distance vision in the dominant eye and good near vision in the nondominant eye. If a postoperative refraction of –1.50 D is desired in a patient who has a preoperative refraction of –5.0 D, then a correction of –3.50 D needs to be programmed into the laser. All patients being evaluated for a surgical monovision correction should initially try monovision contact lenses to ensure they can tolerate the anisometropia and visual quality of monovision and to confirm the preferred distance and near eye.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has a refractive surprise after cataract surgery. He had laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) years before the current surgery. What measurement is most likely the cause of the refractive surprise?

options.a: Lens thickness measurements inaccurately reflect postoperative effective IOL position.
options.b: Axial length measurements inaccurately reflect axial length.
options.c: Keratometry measurements inaccurately reflect corneal refractive power.
options.d: Anterior chamber depth measurements inaccurately reflect postoperative intraocular lens (IOL) position.

pool.rationale: Measurements of axial length, anterior chamber depth, lens thickness, and IOL position should not be affected by LASIK. The keratometric power of the postrefractive surgery cornea is problematic, since the effective central optical zones can be small. This can lead to inaccurate measurements because the keratometers measure the corneal curvature several millimeters away from the center of the cornea. In addition, the relationship between the anterior and posterior corneal curvatures can be considerably altered.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What oral medication, when used after photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), can adversely affect the outcome?
pool.rationale: Oral antihistamines and hormone replacement therapy may delay epithelial healing in patients undergoing PRK. Sumatriptan may also delay epithelial healing in patients undergoing PRK or LASIK. Oral fluoroquinolones, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are less likely to interfere with epithelial healing.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What complication is commonly seen after radial keratotomy?
pool.rationale: Issues with night vision such as glare and halos are the result of light scattering off the incisions/scars. These complications are fairly common following radial keratotomy (RK). While secondary glaucoma is associated with steroid use, it is not associated with radial keratotomy. While corneal ectasia can be seen after RK, it is uncommon and the vast majority of patients do not develop this problem. Cystoid macular edema is associated with intraocular surgery and not RK.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A myopic patient shows 1.5 D more myopia on his wavefront measurement than on his manifest refraction. What is the most likely explanation for this discrepancy?

options.a: The patient was undercorrected on his manifest refraction.
options.b: This is normal, because it is within the margin of error.
options.c: Cyclopentolate drops were given prior to wavefront analysis.

pool.rationale: A wavefront analysis that is 1.5 D more myopic than a patient's manifest refraction is most likely due to patient accommodation during analysis. The wavefront analysis and manifest refraction should be within 0.75 D of each other; otherwise, they should both be repeated. Following cycloplegia, a patient will not demonstrate increased myopia on wavefront analysis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the Munnerlyn formula used for in surgical planning?

options.a: calculating the optical zone diameter for myopic laser refractive surgery
options.b: estimating the amount of cornea tissue removed in myopic laser refractive surgery
options.c: calculating the flap thickness for myopic LASIK
options.d: calculating the flap thickness for hyperopic LASIK

pool.rationale: The Munnerlyn formula is used to estimate the amount of tissue removed centrally: Ablation depth in micrometers ≈ diopters of myopia multiplied by the square of the optical zone diameter divided by 3.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What does the term coupling refer to within refractive surgery?

options.a: the amount of corneal flattening that is observed after myopic photorefractive keratectomy
options.b: post-corneal transplant changes that are the result of a double running suture
options.c: the local topographical effects from a radial corneal incision
options.d: the flattening of a cornea in the meridian of a limbal relaxing incision with concurrent steepening in the meridian 90° away

pool.rationale: Tangential and limbal relaxing corneal incisions alter the shape of the cornea by inducing flattening in the meridian of the incision. At the same time, there is a resultant steepening of the cornea 90° away from the incision, an effect termed coupling. With limbal relaxing incisions, the amount of steepening is equal to the amount of flattening, which results in a coupling ratio of 1.0 and no shift in the refractive error (figure). On the other hand, transverse incisions result in overall flattening of the cornea, a hyperopic shift, and a coupling ratio of greater than 1.0. Radial incisions result in localized flattening without steepening 90° away. A double running suture in a corneal transplant does not result in coupling, nor does photorefractive keratectomy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Haze following photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) typically peaks approximately how long after surgery?
pool.rationale: Subepithelial corneal haze develops as a result of epithelial-stromal wound healing and appears several weeks after surface ablation, peaks in intensity at 1 to 2 months, and gradually diminishes or disappears over the following 6 to 12 months.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Corneal topographic measurements obtained using Placido disk technology can be adversely affected by what disorder?
pool.rationale: Placido disk technology is dependent on reflection of rings from the tear film overlying the anterior surface of the cornea. As dry eye causes irregularities of the tear film composition and volume, this can have a major impact on the quality of placido-disk images. As the technique does not measure the lens, lenticular opacities do not affect the measurement. The same is true of corneal endothelial changes (without corneal edema), as the Placido disk only reflects from the anterior cornea.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the optimal refractive procedure for patients with epithelial basement membrane dystrophy?
pool.rationale: There are certain situations in which photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) is preferred over LASIK or other refractive procedures. One of these is a patient with epithelial basement membrane dystrophy. The process of constructing a LASIK flap can result in an abrasion, making PRK the preferred procedure. PRK is preferred in patients with abnormally thin corneas, as well, because they may not have enough stromal bed left behind if LASIK is performed. In abnormally flat or steep corneas, PRK may be the better option, since these patients may be more likely to have an incomplete flap or a buttonhole flap, respectively. Intracorneal ring segments are primarily used in the treatment of keratoconus. Radial keratotomy is no longer widely used.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Why might increasing the optical zone in myopic laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) or photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) limit the ability to treat patients with thinner corneas?

options.a: It increases the risk of postoperative glare and halos.
options.b: It decreases predictability of the refractive outcome.
options.d: It increases the chance of regression.

pool.rationale:
All photoablative procedures result in the removal of corneal tissue. The depth of myopic laser ablation by a broad beam laser is estimated by the Munnerlyn formula.
Ablation depth (microns) = [degree of myopia (D) x (optical zone diameter in mm)^2]/3
As the ablation diameter increases, the depth required for a given refractive correction increases by the optical zone squared. Thus, the difference in the ablation depth increase is not linear and can rapidly exceed the ability of the cornea to structurally handle the ablation depth and still maintain appropriate residual stromal bed thickness. Complications of glare, halos, and regression increase when the optical zone decreases. So increasing the optical zone would actually improve these issues. For this reason, the optical zone should be 6 mm or larger.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 40-year-old soft contact lens wearer presents for a laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) evaluation after discontinuing contact lens use for 2 weeks. A refraction of -5.50 +0.50 X 90 OD and -5.00 sphere OS results in 20/25 acuity in each eye. Keratometry reveals mildly distorted mires, and slit-lamp examination is normal except for peripheral, superficial neovascularization of the cornea. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.c: Prescribe artificial tears, recommend continued contact lens abstinence, and reevaluate the patient in a few weeks.
options.d: Ask the patient to return for a repeat examination with contact lenses in place to check fit and vision.

pool.rationale: Contact lens use can change the shape of the cornea, especially with long-term wear. The exact amount of time required for the cornea to assume its natural shape after discontinuation of contact lens wear varies from patient to patient. If a patient's corneas are still irregular after a few weeks of discontinuation, the patient should be followed (while continuing to abstain from contact lens wear) until the cornea has stabilized. Proceeding with refractive surgery in this scenario would jeopardize a good and stable outcome. Reevaluating the fit is appropriate in a patient who wants to continue wearing contact lenses.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following creation and lifting of the flap during laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), a patient has intraoperative difficulty identifying the fixation target. The ablation is completed. After surgery, the patient complains of glare and halos that are not improved with refraction. The slit-lamp examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely cause of the patient's complaints?
pool.rationale: Decentered ablation may occur if the patient's eye drifts and loses fixation, if the head is positioned improperly, or if the eye is not perpendicular to the treatment laser. Centration is even more critical in hyperopic ablations and with higher refractive correction. Over- and undercorrection would be improved with refraction. Diffuse lamellar keratitis would be noted on a slit-lamp examination.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient requests refractive surgical correction of his left eye. He reports that he has had laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) previously on his right eye (shown). What preoperative risk factor could the ophthalmologist anticipate to avoid repeating this complication?
pool.rationale:
Steep keratometry is associated with an increased incidence of buttonhole flaps with mechanical microkeratomes. Buttonhole flaps may occur when more cornea is pushed up through the suction ring, leading to a larger area of applanation than is possible for the cornea, which in turn leads to posterior movement of the cornea and a thin central flap. Other causes are poor suction or problems with the blade.
Thick corneas are not an independent risk factor for buttonholes. Though EBMD may increase the incidence of epithelial defects and epithelial ingrowth, it is not a cause of buttonhole flaps.
Shallow orbits improve exposure, and make it less likely to have suction loss. Suction loss is a risk factor for buttonholes, but not shallow orbits.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What wavelength of energy, when applied to the cornea, is characterized by high energy and precision, low penetration of tissue, and limited thermal spread?
pool.rationale: A variety of laser-tissue interactions are used in keratorefractive surgery. Argon-fluoride excimer laser generates a wavelength of 193 nm with high energy and precision but low tissue penetrance and little thermal spread, making this laser highly suitable for use on the ocular surface. Thus, excimer laser photoablation at 193 nm is the correct answer choice. Femtosecond laser generates a wavelength of 1053 nm that causes photodisruption, which transforms tissue into plasma with high pressure and temperature and leads to rapid tissue expansion. This creates microscopic cavities that are useful in the creation of stromal flaps and channels. Holmium-YAG laser creates a wavelength of 2.13 µm that causes a photothermal effect. When applied to the anterior stroma, water in the cornea absorbs the energy and creates heat that shrinks surrounding collagen. This is useful in the creation of corneal flattening at the anterior surface, and this technique (laser thermokeratoplasty [LTK]) is approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of low hyperopia. Collagen cross-linking units create a wavelength of 365 nm (ultraviolet A) that, while not used in refractive surgery, is used the treatment of corneal ectasia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Night-vision problems following myopic laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) are most likely to result from what condition?
pool.rationale: Common night vision problems like glare and halos can result after laser vision correction as a result of increased higher order aberrations, specifically, spherical aberration. Large, well-centered uniform optical zones provide better quality of vision, especially at night. Thin corneas are less likely to be associated with night-vision problems.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is an advantage of arcuate keratotomy (AK) over limbal relaxing incisions (LRIs)?

options.a: Arcuate keratotomy incisions can be shorter than limbal relaxing incisions to correct the same amount of astigmatism.
options.b: Arcuate keratotomy incisions have less risk of irregular astigmatism than limbal relaxing incisions.
options.c: Arcuate keratotomy incisions can be performed with a standard cataract keratome knife.
options.d: Arcuate keratotomy incisions can also correct higher-order corneal aberrations.

pool.rationale: Both AKs and LRIs are incisional corneal techniques used to correct corneal astigmatism. The more central location of AKs allows for a larger amount of astigmatic correction with a smaller corneal arc length incision than an LRI. AKs are typically performed at the 7-9 mm optical zone to 95% corneal depth. LRIs are typically performed just anterior to the limbus at a depth of 600 microns. Both incisional techniques take advantage of a coupling ratio of 1.0 with minimal risk of substantial hyperopic shift. Both AKs and LRIs are generally performed with diamond blades, although surgeons more frequently use an adjustable rather than a preset blade when performing AKs. Irregular astigmatism is possible with both AKs and LRIs, although it is more common with AKs, given the closer proximity of the relaxing incision to the optical zone. Neither technique can be used reliably to correct higher-order aberrations.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What refractive procedure is most likely to cause surgically induced ectasia?

options.a: intrastromal corneal ring segments (ICRS; Intacs and Ferrara rings)

pool.rationale:
Ectasia is far more common after LASIK than after PRK. This is related to the residual stromal bed thickness (RSBT), which is far less with LASIK flap creation than with surface ablation.
Intacs is a treatment designed to reduce the irregular astigmatic error from ectasia, but it cannot prevent ectasia progression. Epikeratophakia, a largely obsolete procedure, featured the suturing of a donor lenticule on top of the Bowman layer of the host cornea and was designed as a "living contact lens" for those patients who were unable to wear contact lenses, including patients with keratoconus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For preoperative planning purposes of laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), what is the minimum residual stromal bed thickness?
pool.rationale: The recommended minimal residual stromal bed thickness is 250 microns. Leaving a residual stromal bed of less than 250 µm might place the patient at higher risk of developing corneal ectasia after LASIK surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the primary difference between femtosecond lenticule extraction (FLEx) and small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE)?
pool.rationale: The SMILE method is performed entirely within a pocket, avoiding the need for a flap. Both methods use a femtosecond laser, can be used for correcting myopia, and involve a stromal ablation to create refractive change.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Why are IOL calculations difficult to accurately obtain in someone who has had laser refractive surgery?

options.a: Most traditional keratometers measure only the central corneal curvature.
options.b: The relationship between the anterior and posterior cornea has changed.
options.c: Tear film abnormalities make it difficult to obtain keratometry readings.
options.d: The axial length cannot be accurately measured.

pool.rationale:
Numerous formulas have been developed to help with post-refractive IOL selection, but there is no infallible way, at present, to calculate IOL power due to the nature of the post-refractive cornea. Standard IOL calculations make certain assumptions about the relationship between the anterior and posterior curvatures of the cornea, which is altered post ablation. Additionally, the effective central optic zone after refractive surgery is typically small (imagine a flatter central cornea after post-myopic LASIK with preserved natural peripheral corneal curvature), and most keratometers measure corneal curvature several millimeters away from the center of the cornea, which results in inaccurate estimation of the true central corneal power. In general, refractive surgery for myopia results in a hyperopic surprise post cataract surgery; refractive surgery for hyperopia results in a myopic surprise.
The axial eye length (AEL) does not change after laser refractive surgery, and AEL measurements should remain accurate. Some formulas rely on keratometry to estimate the effective lens position, which may be inaccurately estimated (as described above), resulting in errors, depending on which IOL formula is used. Tear film abnormalities may make it difficult to obtain keratometry readings; however, this effect, if properly treated, does not contribute errors to the IOL calculations.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During bilateral laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) surgery, a buttonhole occurs during flap creation in the first eye. What is the best course of action?

options.a: Replace the flap and proceed as planned with the second eye.
options.b: Replace the flap, set the microkeratome deeper, and repeat flap creation and perform the ablation on this eye, then on the second eye in similar fashion.
options.c: Replace the flap and perform a surface ablation on the second eye.
options.d: Replace the flap and abort the procedure for the second eye.

pool.rationale:
Buttonhole flaps can result in irregular astigmatism with loss of best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), and steep corneal curvature is a risk factor. If a thin or buttonhole flap is created, the flap should be replaced and ablation should not be performed. After the flap is replaced, stabilized with a bandage contact lens for several days, and allowed to heal for at least 3 months, a deeper flap can be created or a surface ablation can be performed.
Since the surgical plan may be changed for the contralateral eye, it is best to defer surgery for the second eye.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: One week after photorefractive keratectomy, a pleased and asymptomatic patient has an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/30. Given the patient's appearance shown, what condition fits with the clinical findings?
pool.rationale: This patient has sterile infiltrates following photorefractive keratectomy. This finding is most commonly associated with postoperative contact lens use and topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drop use. The remaining answer choices could result in corneal infiltrates in this patient, but each would likely be symptomatic (ie, pain and photophobia), with conjunctival injection.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Cycloplegic refraction would most likely be recommended for an adult refractive surgery patient in what scenario?

options.a: a patient suspected of accommodating during manifest refraction
options.b: a laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) patient complaining of residual glare
options.c: a keratoconus patient being fitted for contact lenses
options.d: a patient complaining about his current spectacles

pool.rationale: A cycloplegic refraction can be quite helpful for a patient who is suspected of accommodation during the manifest refraction. This condition is more common in younger patients and those with hyperopia. It is especially clinically meaningful in patients who are considering refractive surgery. If the refractive error is surgically corrected based on a refraction where a patient is accommodating, then the result long term may be more myopic than intended. Therefore, it is recommended that all patients under 35 being evaluated for refractive surgery undergo a cycloplegic refraction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A young myopic patient wants laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) surgery. Manifest refraction is -4.00 +1.00 X 90 in the right eye. Cycloplegic refraction in the same eye is -3.00 +1.00 X 90. What is the reason for the discrepancy?
pool.rationale: In a patient with refractive error, it is important to understand the refractive state of the eye before performing surgical correction for that refractive error. When the difference between the manifest and cycloplegic refractions is large (eg, >0.50 D), a post-cycloplegic manifest refraction may be helpful to recheck the original. In patients with myopia, such a large difference is often caused by an overminused manifest refraction. In patients with hyperopia, substantial latent hyperopia may be present, in which case the surgeon and patient need to decide exactly how much hyperopia to treat. If there is significant latent hyperopia, a pushed-plus spectacle or contact lens correction can be worn for several weeks or months preoperatively to reduce the postoperative adjustment that may result from treating the true refraction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Historically, what is the minimum recommended residual corneal stromal bed thickness (RSBT) following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?
pool.rationale: Although no definitive laboratory investigations or controlled prospective studies have been done, most practitioners use a minimum RSBT of 250 µm as a guideline. RSBT is calculated as the central corneal thickness less the depth of ablation and the thickness of the LASIK flap (when applicable). A thicker stromal bed after ablation does not guarantee that postoperative corneal ectasia will not develop. Microkeratome-created LASIK flaps may be thicker than noted on the label of the microkeratome head, making the RSBT thinner than calculated and increasing the risk of a thinner than intended RSBT. This can be detected by intraoperative pachymetry of the untreated stromal bed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Femtosecond lasers separate tissue through photodisruption, utilizing wavelengths within what electromagnetic band?
pool.rationale: In keratorefractive surgery there are 3 different types of laser-tissue interactions: photoablative, photodisruptive, and photothermal. Femtosecond lasers used in flap creation in laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) have a wavelength of 1053 nm. This places them in the infrared spectrum. They are not in the visible, microwave, or ultraviolet spectrum. The infrared beam causes photodisruption (a process by which tissue is transformed into plasma). With the high pressure and temperature generated, this creates microscopic cavities within the corneal stroma. Contiguous photodisruption during LASIK allows creation of the corneal flap. This type of photodisruptive effect can also create a lenticule of tissue, a channel, or a keratoplasty incision for various other refractive procedures.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: To improve vision associated with myopic astigmatism caused by post-LASIK corneal ectasia, what is an appropriate initial option?
pool.rationale: RGP contact lenses are the gold standard for the correction of reduced vision due to ectasia. Surgical procedures that thin or destabilize the cornea (eg, LASIK, PRK, incisional procedures) might complicate the situation further. Ectasia might be progressive, so refractive lens exchange is also contraindicated. Because the contact lens fit and power can be modified as the ectasia progresses, RGP contact lenses are the most appropriate treatment. In the future, corneal crosslinking might become the treatment of choice to prevent further ectasia, but it does not improve vision as much as RGP contact lenses.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What complication of radial keratotomy (RK) typically occurs 10 years or more after the procedure?
pool.rationale: Progressive hyperopia is a common long-term complication due to progressive central corneal flattening after RK resulting from peripheral corneal instability. The Prospective Evaluation of Radial Keratotomy (PERK) study found that 43% of eyes undergoing RK developed progressive hyperopia and were overcorrected by more than 1.00 diopters at 10 years postoperatively. Loss of best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA; also called corrected distance visual acuity, CDVA) secondary to nuclear sclerotic cataract can occur after RK surgery; however, this usually occurs secondary to aging and is not related to the procedure itself. Increased intraocular pressure is a rare complication that can occur secondary to treatment with topical corticosteroids in the early postoperative period. Globe perforation is a rare complication that can occur during the RK procedure and with less likelihood thereafter.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In wavefront analysis, what type of optical aberration is coma?
pool.rationale:
Optical aberrations measured by wavefront analyzers, such as the Hartmann-Shack wavefront sensor, can be described by an infinite number of systems.  One set of descriptors are Zernike polynomials, which are the mathematical formulas used to describe surfaces.
Lower-order (second-order) aberrations include myopia, hyperopia, and regular astigmatism. Myopia produces positive defocus, hyperopia produces negative defocus, and regular (cylindrical) astigmatism produces a wavefront aberration that has orthogonal and oblique components.
The most important Zernike coefficients affecting visual quality are coma, trefoil, and spherical aberration. Coma and trefoil are third-order aberrations. With coma, light rays at one edge of the pupil come into focus before rays at the opposite edge; the effective image resembles a comet, having vertical and horizontal components. Coma is common in patients with decentered corneal grafts, keratoconus, and decentered laser ablations.
Spherical aberration, a fourth-order aberration, is the most clinically significant higher-order aberration. It increases depth of field, but decreases contrast sensitivity, causes night myopia, results in halos around point images, and is commonly increased after myopic laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) and surface ablation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What have clinical trials on conductive keratoplasty demonstrated regarding the long-term effectiveness and stability of this procedure?

options.a: Myopic progression was found in hyperopic and presbyopic patients.
options.b: Both hyperopic and presbyopic patients remained stable at 1 to 2 years.
options.c: Regression was found in treatment of hyperopia and presbyopia.
options.d: Unpredictable results were seen in patients with more than 3.00 D of hyperopia.

pool.rationale: The clinical trial results for conductive keratoplasty treatment in patients with hyperopia were similar to those of patients with presbyopia, in that there was initial improvement with loss of effect over 2 years in the hyperopic population and over 1 year in the presbyopic population. The upper limit of treatment appears to be +3.25 D, beyond which there does not appear to be any enhanced effect with additional treatment. Trials have shown a loss of effect of 20% after 2 years for hyperopic and presbyopic treatments. Regression with a return to the baseline amount of hyperopia or presbyopia has been observed as opposed to any myopic progression.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: One day after laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), a patient is found to have blurred vision in one eye. The slit-lamp appearance of the flap is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Macrostriae are full-thickness undulating stromal folds that can cause decreased vision after LASIK, the majority of which are present on the first postoperative day. They may develop due to initial flap malposition or postoperative flap slippage. Repositioning of the flap should be performed immediately before epithelial hyperplasia can occur.

Microstriae are small folds in the Bowman layer that appear as fine hairlike irregularities and are less likely to affect vision. Epithelial ingrowth would occur later in the postoperative course. With DLK, the inflammatory cells in the interface have a different appearance than in the images above.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a risk factor for delayed epithelial healing after photorefractive keratectomy (PRK)?
pool.rationale: Patients with ocular surface disease may have problems with epithelial healing. This is especially true in patients with large epithelial defects that occur after surface ablation procedures, such as PRK.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient who has undergone penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) presents for evaluation of laser refractive surgery. What would be a contraindication to performing laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) in this patient?

options.a: poor visual potential in the contralateral eye
options.d: regular astigmatism centrally, but irregular astigmatism peripherally

pool.rationale:
Poor visual potential in the contralateral eye would be a relative contraindication to performing LASIK on a post-PKP eye. Patients with wound-healing disorders, collagen vascular diseases, low endothelial cell counts, and significant dry eye would also be poor candidates for LASIK after PKP.
LASIK can be performed for a high degree of myopia, provided that usual criteria are met, such as the thickness of the residual stromal bed. The goal of LASIK in a post-PKP eye would be to return the patient to good spectacle-corrected acuity.
Regular astigmatism centrally is amenable to treatment by LASIK in a post-PKP eye.
EBMD is not a contraindication to LASIK, although it may be preferable to perform photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), provided that there are no other contraindications.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 48-year-old woman had uncomplicated bilateral laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). One month after the procedure, she notes blurred and fluctuating vision. Examination reveals diffuse corneal punctate epitheliopathy in the interpalpebral fissure. What is the preferred initial therapy?

options.a: frequent application of preservative-free artificial tears
options.c: frequent application of topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents

pool.rationale:
Dry eye, a frequent transient adverse effect after LASIK, is the most likely cause of this patient's signs and symptoms. The preferred initial treatment is to address the underlying disorder with frequent application of preservative-free tears.
Frequent application of antibiotics is not preferred because the patient exhibits no signs of infection.
Frequent application of topical steroid drops would not be indicated, because there is no evidence of inflammation.
Frequent application of topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents is not a preferred treatment for dry eyes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 45-year-old man develops grade 1 reticular haze 4 weeks after bilateral photorefractive keratectomy (PRK). His vision is only mildly decreased. What is the most appropriate initial management?
pool.rationale:
Haze typically appears several weeks after surface ablation, peaks at 1–2 months, and then gradually diminishes or disappears over the next 6–12 months. Increasing steroid drops might help the patient, whereas nonsteroidal drops would have limited benefit.

Topical mitomycin C therapy is not indicated. Repeat ablation with mitomycin C can be performed at a later time if the haze does not resolve or the patient has more severe haze with unacceptable vision.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What condition are corneal inlays approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to treat?
pool.rationale: Corneal inlays improve near vision by changing corneal curvature, increasing depth of field via a small central aperture, or changing the refractive index of the cornea.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 65-year-old woman undergoes cataract surgery with implantation of a multifocal IOL (MFIOL). Two weeks postoperatively, she notes that she is experiencing glare and halos around lights at night. What next step is her management?

options.c: Remove and replace the MFIOL with a monofocal IOL because the multifocal lens is probably causing the halos and glare.
options.d: Plan a return to the operating room to reposition the IOL because decentration might be the cause.

pool.rationale: Patients with suboptimal results or who are dissatisfied with the quality of vision after multifocal lens implantation should first undergo a comprehensive evaluation, from the ocular surface to the macula, to rule out dry eyes, residual refractive error, irregular astigmatism, cystoid macular edema, and epiretinal membrane. Decentration of the IOL, unless significant and obvious, should not be addressed as the first-line treatment, as the intervention is invasive and may be avoidable. Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy should be considered only if other causes have been ruled out because the opening of the capsule will then cause a significant challenge if IOL exchange becomes necessary.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) is recommended over laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) for what preoperative condition?
pool.rationale: The presence of a flap in LASIK will yield a lower residual stromal bed than PRK for a given treatment. Thus, for a thin cornea, PRK is preferred over LASIK to achieve an adequate residual stromal bed and reduce the risk of postrefractive ectasia. Although Salzmann nodular degeneration could conceivably be addressed by nodulectomy prior to refractive surgery using either technique, the decision to perform PRK or LASIK in this condition also should be considered carefully, due to the risk of nodule recurrence. Narrow, not wide, palpebral fissures make surface ablation a better choice, as creating the LASIK flap becomes more difficult with a narrow palpebral fissure. The risk of post-procedure haze in high myopes is greater with surface ablation than with LASIK.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient experiences pain and light sensitivity 2 months after femtosecond-assisted laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). The eye appears white and quiet. What is the best initial treatment?

options.a: flap lift and irrigation of the lamellar space with sterile saline
options.c: flap lift with culture for suspected microbial keratitis

pool.rationale: Good acuity, postoperative photophobia is a rare entity that can occur weeks to months after LASIK. Patients develop acute onset of pain and photophobia in a white and quiet eye in which both the cornea and the flap interface appear normal. The treatment consists of frequent application of topical corticosteroids and cyclosporine A. The flap does not have to be touched.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most likely etiology of a focal white cell infiltrate in the flap interface that develops 2 days following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?
pool.rationale:
Staphylococcus aureus

Fortunately, infectious keratitis following refractive surgery is very infrequent. Careful attention to cleansing the lids may be useful in reducing the frequency of infectious keratitis. If an infiltrate occurs, then the time course of the appearance of the infection can often give some clue to the nature of the infectious organism. Typically, early infections (such as in this example on day 2) are bacterial. Fungal and mycobacterial infections typically occur later after the surgery than the bacterial infections. Nocardia is a gram-positive bacterium, yet has lower virulence than other species, and therefore typically will present later after the surgical procedure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Wavefront analysis based on the Hartmann-Shack wavefront sensor is affected by what ocular structures?

options.b: cornea, anterior chamber, lens, and vitreous

pool.rationale: Wavefront analysis based on the Hartmann-Shack wavefront sensor uses a low-power laser beam that is focused on the retina. The reflected light is propagated back through the optical elements of the eye (vitreous, lens, anterior chamber, cornea), captured by a sensor, and analyzed. Thus all elements affect the analysis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: One week following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), a patient has the findings shown in the figure. What is the most appropriate management for this complication?

options.a: Observation is appropriate if there is no progression.
options.b: Lift the flap and mechanically remove the epithelium.
options.c: Lift the flap and irrigate with using alcohol to facilitate removal of the epithelium.
options.d: Lift the flap and irrigate with mitomycin C to facilitate removal of the epithelium.

pool.rationale:
Epithelial ingrowth after LASIK can be observed in the early postoperative period if it is in the peripheral 1-2 mm, because it typically does not progress and is not generally clinically significant.
If it progresses to become visually significant (causing irregular astigmatism or glare due to its location in or abutting the visual axis), causes significant foreign body sensation or irritation, or induces keratolysis, flap-lifting is indicated. Initial surgical treatment for epithelial ingrowth is performed with a flap lift, removal of epithelial cells from the posterior surface of the flap and the stromal bed with a blade or similar instrument, and replacement of the flap without sutures or tissue glue. Subsequent surgical treatment for recurrent episodes of epithelial ingrowth includes flap-lifting with additional measures taken, including flap suture, fibrin glue, or YAG laser treatment. Treatment with agents, such as alcohol and mitomycin, can cause complications from keratocyte death, including flap-melting, and should be approached cautiously.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For about a year, a 39-year-old patient who has never worn glasses or contact lenses has had blurry vision at near greater than distance. Slit-lamp and fundus examinations are normal. What diagnostic examination would confirm the ophthalmologist's working diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
An early onset of presbyopia symptoms should trigger recognition of possible (latent) hyperopia and loss of accommodation. A cycloplegic refraction would confirm hyperopia.
Corneal ectasia would be detected by characteristic slit-lamp examination findings (eg, apical thinning with possible Vogt striae and Fleischer ring in keratoconus) and irregular astigmatism on corneal topography, and ectasia would be expected to manifest as visual distortion at all refractive distances not corrected by spectacles.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What medical history finding in a 25-year-old man would be a relative contraindication for laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?
pool.rationale:
Immunocompromised status, including HIV/AIDS, represents a relative contraindication to refractive surgery due to the potential for increased risk of infectious complications. The FDA recommends that patients with an immunodeficiency disease not undergo LASIK because the risk outweighs the benefits.

The remaining choices do not represent contraindicated states, but it is important to assess for associated disease states with each: atopy in the case of asthma, optic neuritis in the case of MS, and dry-eye disease with antidepressant use in the case of depression.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 48-year-old woman has a persistent central corneal epithelial defect 2 weeks after photorefractive keratectomy. She has a bandage soft contact lens in place and is using preservative-free artificial tear drops and topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) every 2 hours. Her Schirmer test scores are normal. What is the best initial management option?

options.a: Add topical cyclosporine 0.05% eye drops 2 times daily.
options.c: Add topical prednisolone acetate 1% eye drops 4 times daily.
options.d: Place a lower eyelid punctal plug.

pool.rationale: Topical NSAIDs can be applied after surface ablation to reduce postoperative pain, but topical NSAID drops can slow epithelialization and result in corneal melting, stromal scarring, and irregular astigmatism. Corneal epithelial defects after surface ablation typically heal in 3 to 4 days postoperatively. For any patient not healing normally after refractive surgery, topical NSAID drops should be discontinued. A frequent cause of delayed epithelialization is keratoconjunctivitis sicca, which can be treated with increased lubrication, topical cyclosporine, and/or temporary punctal occlusion; however, this patient has normal Schirmer test scores and is already receiving frequent preservative-free artificial tears, so these measures are not indicated as first-line treatments. Topical steroidal antiinflammatory drops, such as prednisolone acetate, will not likely result in improved epithelialization in this case.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What condition can alloplastic corneal inlays be used to treat?
pool.rationale: Alloplastic corneal inlays can be used to treat presbyopic patients. These inlays have several potential advantages over homoplastic inlays, such as the ability to be accurately mass-produced in a wide range of sizes and powers. Four different presbyopic inlays have been developed and are currently in investigational studies. In 2015, the United States Food and Drug Administration approved the small-aperture KAMRA corneal inlay (AcuFocus Inc, Irvine, CA) for the improvement of near vision in presbyopic patients who require near correction.

pool.q: In an evaluation for refractive surgery, what feature of the cornea is best determined by Placido disk topography?
pool.rationale: Placido disk topography permits an evaluation of the corneal curvature by providing information about corneal elevation and keratometric power. Irregular astigmatism can be determined by Placido disk topography. Patients with visually significant irregular astigmatism are generally not good candidates for refractive surgery, and when this astigmatism is detected, the cause should be investigated and addressed. Higher-order aberrations can be detected by wavefront analysis. Residual bed thickness is calculated using the central corneal pachymetry (determined by properly calibrated ultrasonography or optical coherence tomography units) by subtracting the flap thickness and ablation depth from the patient’s refraction. Posterior corneal curvature is measured by optical coherence tomography.

pool.q: When offering monovision to a patient who desires near and distance vision with contact lenses, refractive surgery, or cataract surgery, what refractive error differential typically provides a well-tolerated balance of distance and near vision?

options.a: The dominant eye is corrected for distance and the nondominant eye with a target refraction of –0.50 D.
options.b: The dominant eye is corrected for distance and the nondominant eye with a target refraction of –1.25 D to –2.50 D.
options.c: The nondominant eye is corrected for distance and the dominant eye with a target refraction of –0.50 D.
options.d: The nondominant eye is corrected for distance and the dominant eye with a target refraction of –3.25 D.

pool.rationale: Monovision can be attempted with contact lenses, LASIK, PRK, or cataract surgery. It is typically done by correcting the dominant eye for distant focus and designating the nondominant eye as the near eye with a refractive error of –1.50 to –2.50 D. Before performing a monovision refractive treatment in a patient who has never experienced monovision, the patient should trial contact lenses with the planned monofocal correction to ensure the patient can tolerate monovision. Some patients prefer their nondominant eye for distance, and others prefer their dominant eye. Many patients do not tolerate adequate anisometropia to allow for adequate near vision and therefore should typically not undergo refractive surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What perioperative consideration of myopic excimer laser refractive surgery increases the risk for overcorrection?
pool.rationale:
Overcorrection may occur if substantial stromal dehydration develops before the laser treatment is initiated, because more tissue will be ablated per pulse. Older patients, as compared to younger patients, tend to experience overcorrection because their wound healing response is less vigorous and their corneas ablate at a greater rate, for unknown reasons.
Epithelial hyperplasia and postrefractive ectasia are associated with the potential for greater keratometric power and myopic shifting after myopic ablation.

pool.q: The ophthalmologist has obtained informed consent from a 40-year-old patient who is scheduled for laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) treatment for -6.00 D OU. The patient has a regular topography and a central corneal thickness (CCT) of 560 μm OU. His intraocular pressure (IOP) is 20 mm Hg, and results of the fundus examination are within normal limits. What outcome is both likely to occur and will have an effect on patient satisfaction?

options.a: The patient will have corneal haze postoperatively.
options.b: There will be a dramatic elevation of IOP during the procedure.
options.c: The patient will have corneal ectasia postoperatively.
options.d: The patient will have difficulty with tasks at near after the procedure.

pool.rationale:
A balanced discussion of the risks, benefits, and alternatives is an important part of informed consent. Patients who are approaching presbyopia, if made emmetropic, will require reading glasses for all near activities. This is crucial to emphasize: It will definitely occur and will affect patient satisfaction postoperatively if the patient is not prepared.
Dramatic elevation of IOP does occur during the procedure, but is unlikely to have any consequence in a normal patient without signs of glaucoma.
Corneal ectasia is not likely to occur in a patient with thick corneas, normal topography, and the amount of treatment described.
Corneal haze is a risk for patients undergoing photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) with treatments of over -4.00, but it is not typically seen in LASIK.

pool.q: A patient develops a persistent epithelial defect with keratolysis after uneventful photorefractive keratectomy (PRK). She has no prior history of ocular infections or ophthalmic problems preoperatively. The use of what concentration of mitomycin C would likely contribute to this complication?
pool.rationale: Mitomycin C is used in photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) to reduce the formation of corneal haze postoperatively. During the procedure, a pledget soaked in mitomycin C – usually 0.02% or 0.2 mg/mL – is placed on the ablated surface for 12 seconds to 2 minutes. The duration of mitomycin C application may vary by diagnosis and surgeon preference. However, it is important to use an appropriately low-dose concentration of mitomycin C (0.02% or less) and irrigate the ocular surface copiously afterward to prevent complications of its use, which include persistent epithelial defects, corneal melting, and endothelial cell toxicity. There have been no cases of corneal melt reported after the single use of low-dose mitomycin C (0.02% or less) during a PRK procedure.

pool.q: A 26-year-old patient undergoes laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) for the treatment of -9.00 D myopia. The ophthalmologist notes slightly decreased vision and glare symptoms 1 week postoperatively. The examination is normal with the exception of flap striae. What is the most likely cause of the striae?
pool.rationale:
When present, 95% of flap striae are noted by 1 week postoperatively. Risk factors include excessive irrigation under the flap at the time of surgery, thin flaps, or large ablations with subsequent mismatch of the flap to the underlying stroma. In this clinical situation, the striae are most likely due to the high myopic treatment.
DLK presents with haze near the edge of the flap to central diffuse haze. It can occur after a primary procedure or after flap lift or trauma. It is an inflammatory process that results in the accumulation of white blood cells in the interface. DLK does not present as flap striae.
Ectasia does not occur at 1 week postoperatively, and does not present as striae.
Ingrowth is more likely to occur in patients with an epithelial defect at the time of surgery or after re-treatments.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Deep orbits and narrow interpalpebral fissures are a risk factor for what complication during laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?

options.a: irregular laser ablation with irregular astigmatism
options.d: loss of suction with incomplete flap

pool.rationale:
Loss of suction can lead to complications of flap creation, including incomplete flap formation. Careful attention should be paid in the preoperative exam to the patient’s orbital anatomy and the position of the globe within the orbit. A prominent orbital ridge or brow, enophthalmos, or narrow palpebral fissures can make it difficult to achieve and maintain suction, whether using an applanation cone and femtosecond laser or a microkeratome head and blade to create the flap.
The patient’s head should be positioned for comfort and centration prior to docking the cone or microkeratome head to ensure proper centration and avoid irregular and/or off-centered ablation due to improper head positioning.

Epithelial ingrowth can result from sloughing of epithelium during flap creation or suboptimal flap repositioning, and although preoperative basement membrane dystrophy is a risk factor, orbital/periadnexal anatomy and incomplete flap formation are not. Deep orbits and narrow fissures are not a risk factor for corneal haze.
