pool.q: What is a common late complication of radial keratotomy (RK)?

options.a: progressive reduction in size of the optical zone

pool.rationale:
To evaluate the safety and efficacy of RK, the Prospective Evaluation of Radial Keratotomy (PERK) study was undertaken in 1982 for patients with myopia from –2.00 D to –8.75 D (mean, –3.875 D). The most important finding in the 10-year PERK study was the continuing long-term instability of the procedure. A hyperopic shift of 1.00 D or greater was found in 43% of eyes between 6 months and 10 years postoperatively. Most eyes were generally stable by 3 months after RK surgery. However, diurnal fluctuation of vision and a progressive flattening effect after surgery have been known to persist, resulting in refractive instability. Diurnal fluctuation of vision occurs due to hypoxic edema of the incisions with the eyelids closed during sleep. This edema causes flattening of the cornea (and hyperopic shift) upon awakening, followed by steepening later in the day. The optical zone does not change over time.
Small, effective central optical zones after RK can lead to inaccurate measurements because keratometers and Placido disk–based corneal topography units measure the corneal curvature several millimeters away from the center of the cornea and possibly outside the modified treated zone. Generally, if standard keratometry readings are used to calculate IOL power for a previously myopic, postrefractive surgery eye, the postoperative refractive error will be hyperopic, because the keratometry readings are erroneously steeper than the true central corneal power.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the shape of the normal human corneal anterior surface?
pool.rationale: The typical cornea is prolate, which is a description of the asphericity of the cornea. The typical cornea is steeper in the center, and flatter in the periphery. An oblate cornea occurs in situations such as a prior myopic laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) or photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), where the central cornea is flatter than the periphery. A typical cornea has positive asphericity.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is an advantage of using a corneal inlay to treat refractive error or presbyopia?

options.a: It does not require creation of a flap or pocket.
options.b: There is no contrast sensitivity loss in dim illumination.

pool.rationale: Corneal inlays are typically placed into a corneal stromal pocket created by a femtosecond laser. They can be removed and are thus partially reversible, since the flap persists after removal of the inlays. Side effects include decreased contrast sensitivity, as well as glare and haloes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 33-year-old woman presents for evaluation for laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). She has a medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and asthma and is currently 12 weeks into her first pregnancy. Her diabetes and hypertension are well-controlled and she has no retinopathy. Her asthma is also well-controlled with infrequent flare-ups. Her pregnancy has been unremarkable and she is feeling well. Which of her conditions is generally a contraindication to LASIK?
pool.rationale:
Refractive surgery is generally contraindicated in pregnant and nursing women because of possible changes in refraction and corneal hydration. Most surgeons advise waiting at least 3 months after delivery and cessation of nursing before performing an evaluation for refractive surgery.
Most other systemic conditions should be controlled before proceeding with refractive surgery. In patients with well-controlled, stable hypertension without active retinopathy, LASIK is typically quite safe. In patients with controlled asthma, LASIK is also quite safe, yet careful slit lamp examination for cataract should be done, as some of these patients may have had systemic steroids in the past. Because diabetes may cause lens-induced myopia at times of uncontrolled glucose levels, it should be well controlled if LASIK is to be performed. Additionally, cataract and retinal changes may be present that would otherwise be a contraindication for LASIK, but they can be ruled out through examination. People with diabetes may also more commonly have basement membrane changes, and a careful history and examination should be carried out with the attempt to detect the potential for loose epithelium.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has occasional symptoms of double vision that has not required prism-in glasses. The patient has myopia and is interested in being spectacle independent. What testing can be done to evaluate the possibility of strabismus after surgery in this patient before laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) is performed?

options.a: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain

pool.rationale:
Refractive surgery in patients with strabismus or amblyopia requires additional testing in some of these patients. Amblyopia occurs in 2%-4% of the population; up to half of that group has anisometropic amblyopia. Strabismus of small amounts is also common in the population. Persistent diplopia can occur after bilateral LASIK in a patient with anisometropic amblyopia and a history of intermittent diplopia. If the patient is accustomed to the spectacle correction and the resultant image size disparity, this can also cause diplopia from the dissimilar retinal image size.
Patients who have strabismus and wear prism in their glasses may not tolerate refractive surgery without wearing prism in their glasses postoperatively. When faced with this reality, patients may decide that if they still need spectacle correction, they do not wish to undergo refractive surgery. A contact lens trial without prism correction can help to simulate the vision after refractive surgery, and if prisms are still needed over a contact lens, then the patient will likely need prisms also after refractive surgery.
Some patients without prism in their glasses may also need prism after refractive surgery. This group of patients are those that have an abnormal accommodative convergence to accommodation ratio (AC/A). In the myopic patient viewing near objects, spectacles cause a base-in prism effect when converging, and therefore decrease the convergence requirement. In contrast, in a hyperopic patient viewing near objects, spectacles cause a base-out prism effect when converging, and therefore increase the convergence requirement. In patients with an abnormal ability to converge with accommodation, they may experience symptoms in contacts and not glasses, and therefore would notice these symptoms after refractive surgery.
MRI of the brain would not be indicated in a case of intermittent diplopia that is explained by strabismus. Corneal topography would be performed on all patients prior to refractive surgery, but it would not be predictive of patient's postoperative diplopia. Prism spectacles would also not predict diplopia after refractive surgery, as the goal would be independence from spectacles.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Six days after uneventful laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) surgery in the right eye, a 48-year-old patient complains of foggy vision and light sensitivity. Several weeks later he has residual interface scarring, as shown in Figure C. During the development of this complication, what cellular mechanism is most likely to be activated?
pool.rationale: The image depicts diffuse lamellar keratitis (DLK) after LASIK, which is characterized by sterile flap interface inflammation. It is thought to be a nonspecific sterile inflammatory response to a variety of mechanical and/or toxic insults. The flap interface, a potential space, becomes a repository for accumulated leukocytes. Thus, inflammatory cell chemotaxis is the correct answer choice. Epithelial cell injury, such as epithelial defects that occur during primary LASIK or LASIK enhancement, has been described in association with DLK, but epithelial cell injury is not the mechanism for DLK. Leukocyte apoptosis may be involved in the end-stage resolution of DLK. Myofibroblast transformation is not involved in DLK.

pool.q: A patient scheduled for cataract extraction is interested in monovision (one eye corrected for distance and the other eye for near). What clinical test should be performed in the clinic?
pool.rationale:
When considering monovision, determining the patient's dominant eye helps start a discussion about which eye should be corrected for near and which eye should be corrected for distance, as the nondominant eye is often favored for near correction.
Assessments of color vision, binocular fusion, and stereovision are less useful in this scenario.

pool.q: A 45-year-old patient presents wishing to decrease her dependence on reading glasses. She underwent myopic laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) in her 20s. The ophthalmologist discusses monovision with her. What is the best next step?
pool.rationale: Even though a successful monovision trial with contact lens is not a guarantee of a successful outcome after refractive surgery, it is the best and cheapest way for a patient to experience monovision. Glasses are also a possibility but take longer to make and are more expensive. They also would not help the patient achieve her goal of vision without glasses.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 47-year-old, left-eye dominant woman has uncomplicated bilateral laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). Preoperatively, her refraction is -6.00 sphere in each eye. The goal of the LASIK procedure was planned monovision with the right eye for near. Postoperatively, the patient's refraction is -2.50 sphere OD and -0.25+0.50 X 90 OS. Uncorrected, she reads J1+ OD and 20/20 OS. With both eyes open, she reports significant asthenopia when reading and driving. What is the most likely reason for her visual disturbance?

options.a: The difference in the refractive error between the distance and near eyes is too large.
options.b: The patient is too young for monovision.
options.c: The nondominant eye was corrected for distance.
options.d: The residual refractive error in the distance eye is too large.

pool.rationale:
The most common reason for asthenopia or eye strain causing fatigue and headaches is postsurgical anisometropia. She is 20/20 at distance so it is unlikely that the refractive error in her distance eye is too large. She is left-eye dominant, and that is the eye that was corrected for distance. The patient would appreciate some monovision, since she is old enough to have some presbyopia.
Generally, the dominant eye is corrected for distance, and the nondominant eye is corrected to approximately -1.50 to -1.75 D. For most patients, such refraction allows good uncorrected distance and near vision without intolerable anisometropia. Some surgeons prefer a "mini-monovision" procedure, whereby the near-vision eye is corrected to approximately -0.75 D, which allows some near vision with better distance vision and less anisometropia. The exact amount of monovision depends on the desires of the patient. Higher amounts of monovision (up to -2.50 D) can be used successfully in selected patients who want excellent postoperative near vision. However, in some patients with a higher degree of postoperative myopia, improving near vision may lead to unwanted adverse effects of loss of depth perception and anisometropia. It is advisable to have a patient simulate monovision with contact lenses before surgery (generally about 5 days to 1 week, but practices are variable) to ensure that distance and near vision, as well as stereovision, are acceptable and that no muscle imbalance is present, especially with higher degrees of monovision.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What postoperative laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) complication is shown (at low and high magnification) in these images?
pool.rationale: Epithelial ingrowth occurs in a small percentage of eyes undergoing LASIK and is more common in patients who have enhancement procedures. The appearance of epithelial ingrowth is typically cysts of epithelium under the flap, and must be distinguished from meibomian gland material in the flap interface, and epithelial basement membrane dystrophy that is on top of the flap. Management in cases that are progressive to the center of the flap typically involves lifting the flap and removing the epithelial ingrowth.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How are the incisions made when performing limbal relaxing incisions different from the incisions made in astigmatic keratotomy?
pool.rationale: The closer an incision is to the center of the visual axis, the greater the effect on the refractive error of the eye. Astigmatic keratotomy incisions have been made at various optical zones. Limbal relaxing incisions are created closer to the limbus than astigmatic keratotomy incisions. In general, to achieve a similar effect, limbal relaxing incisions should be longer than astigmatic keratotomy incisions, although this is not specific to the definition. Additionally, the cornea is thicker in the periphery, and therefore, in general, incisions should be deeper than the astigmatic keratotomy incision for the equivalent refractive result. The degree of beveling is not specifically different for most surgeons' technique for astigmatic incisions.

pool.q: How long should a pregnant patient wait for laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?

options.a: at least 1 year post-partum and cessation of breastfeeding
options.c: at least 3 months post-partum and cessation of breastfeeding
options.d: good candidate in the first trimester of pregnancy

pool.rationale: When evaluating a patient for photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) or laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), a thorough medical history should be taken, including systemic conditions, prior surgeries, and current/previous medications. Refractive surgery is contraindicated in pregnant and nursing women because changes in corneal hydration may affect refractions. Surgeons often recommend waiting at least 3 months post-partum and cessation of breastfeeding before considering refractive surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 21-year-old patient presents for a laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) evaluation. At his first visit he is wearing 1-year-old glasses that measure -3.00 +1.00 × 25 OD and -3.25 +0.75 × 10 OS. The patient reads 20/25 OD and 20/30 OS. Manifest refraction results in 20/15 acuity in each eye with -3.75 + 1.00 × 180 OD and -3.75 + 1.00 × 170 OS. Cycloplegic refraction confirms the new manifest refraction. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.a: Schedule the patient for LASIK and treat the new manifest refraction.
options.b: Schedule the patient for a repeat evaluation in 6-12 months to ensure the stability of the manifest refraction.
options.c: Schedule the patient for LASIK and treat an additional diopter more than the manifest to compensate for potential progression of myopia.
options.d: Schedule the patient for a repeat examination in 1 month to ensure the stability and accuracy of the manifest refraction.

pool.rationale: There are many important criteria for having a successful outcome with refractive surgery. One of these criteria is to have a stable refractive error. If the refractive error is not stable, and still changing, then if LASIK is performed, when the refractive error changes in the future, the patient will no longer be satisfied with the surgical results. Additionally, a changing refraction can be an indication of other ocular pathology, such as cataract, or corneal ectatic diseases such as keratoconus. Trying to guess the future refractive error is not possible, so the best option is to repeat the refraction several months later.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the appropriate treatment for a buttonhole in a LASIK flap?

options.a: removal of flap followed by PRK at 6 weeks
options.b: replacement of the flap and a bandage contact lens
options.c: removal of flap followed by immediate photorefractive keratotomy (PRK)
options.d: replacement of the flap followed by immediate PRK

pool.rationale: Buttonholes that develop in LASIK flaps as shown (figure) can result in corneal scarring, irregular astigmatism, and loss of best-corrected visual acuity. The appropriate treatment in these cases is to replace the flap if it has been lifted and place a bandage contact lens. The primary risk factor for development of a buttonhole flap is a steep preoperative cornea. At a later date (usually about 3 months), LASIK can be attempted again. It should be noted that a thicker flap should be made to reduce the risk of another flap complication. Alternatively, photorefractive keratectomy can be performed at a later date, rather than immediately. Mitomycin C has no role in the treatment of buttonhole flaps.

pool.q: What complication is associated with posterior chamber phakic intraocular lenses (IOLs)?
pool.rationale: Cataract formation, endothelial cell loss, and retinal detachment have all been seen in patients who undergo posterior chamber phakic IOL implantation. Pupil ovalization was not reported in the U.S. Food and Drug Administration trials and has been more commonly seen in the older anterior chamber IOLs. Hyphema has only been reported with iris-fixated IOLs. Lastly, interlenticular membranes have been observed between 2 artificial lenses, most commonly between 2 acrylic lenses, but not between a patient's natural lens and an artificial lens.

pool.q: A patient complains of fluctuation in vision throughout the day in the first few weeks after laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). What is the most likely cause?
pool.rationale:
The most common cause of fluctuation of vision throughout the day after refractive surgery is dry eye.  Dry eye results from transection of corneal nerves resulting in a neurotrophic cornea. Additionally, corneal surface roughness can contribute to poor tear-film stability.  

Undercorrection and shifting of the flap are issues that cause vision to be poor without correction early in the postoperative period.  Undercorrection is associated with normal best-corrected vision, but striae from a displaced flap can cause poor best-corrected vision.  Diffuse lamellar keratitis is associated early on with normal vision or a mild haze to the vision; if it progresses to stage IV, then permanent irregular astigmatism with decreased best-corrected vision can occur.

pool.q: Following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), what finding would be expected in infectious keratitis that would differentiate it from diffuse lamellar keratitis?

options.c: inflammation extending beyond the flap edge

pool.rationale: Because of the importance for initiating different treatments, distinguishing diffuse lamellar keratitis (DLK) from infectious keratitis is vital following LASIK. The time of onset usually differs among these conditions: infectious keratitis (first figure) will usually present 2 to 3 days after LASIK, while DLK will usually present within the first 24 hours. Decreased vision, conjunctival injection, and photosensitivity are common to both disorders. Inflammation can occur anywhere beneath the flap and can extend above and below the flap interface or beyond the flap edge in cases of infectious keratitis. In contrast, patients with DLK will usually present with inflammation at the periphery of the flap that decreases toward the center. This inflammation remains within the interface (second figure). Both DLK and infectious keratitis can result in flap melts if left untreated.

pool.q: A 62-year-old man underwent myopic photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) 5 years previously. At that time, cup/disc (C/D) ratios measured 0.6 and intraocular pressures measured 21 mm Hg bilaterally. Presently, C/D ratios measure 0.75 and intraocular pressures measure 16 mm Hg bilaterally. What interpretation of the intraocular pressure measurements is correct?

options.a: The actual eye pressure is likely lower than what is measured.
options.b: The actual eye pressure is likely higher than what is measured.
options.c: The present eye pressure indicates that the patient does not have glaucoma.
options.d: The change in C/D ratio is likely due to elevated pressure during the procedure.

pool.rationale:
Because pressure alone is not diagnostic of glaucoma, it is not possible with the pressure alone to diagnose glaucoma in this patient. Thus, the current eye pressure, on its own, does not preclude that the patient has glaucoma. Even though the pressure is one that is often considered in the normal range, there are other factors to consider.
The fact that the patient has had laser vision correction with thinning of the central cornea does influence the accuracy of pressure measurements made through applanation. Goldmann applanation pressures measure lower in thinner corneas and higher in thicker corneas. In this question, we do not know the thickness of the eye, but we know that it is thinner than it was before myopic laser vision correction. Thus, the pressure should actually measure lower (not higher) than the actual values. Glaucoma, however, is a complex diagnosis that requires analysis of the nerve fiber layer, visual field, and optic nerve, as well as comparison with prior information.
There is an elevation from the suction ring during laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) procedures, but the elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) is temporary and unlikely to significantly alter the C/D ratio. The question stem specifically states that this patient underwent PRK, and therefore no significant IOP spike during the procedure is expected.

pool.q: For a patient with an iris-fixated phakic IOL (figure), what post-IOL implantation complication is least likely?
pool.rationale: Although iris-fixated, phakic IOLs have low complication rates, they are not without risks and complications. However, because these lenses are placed in front of the iris, cataract formation is rare. Endothelial cell loss is commonly detected. Glare, starbursts, and halos frequently develop after surgery, but typically improve over time. Dislocation of the lens was seen in a small portion of patients in US Food and Drug Administration clinical trials.

pool.q: Higher-order aberration correction is associated with what form of ablation profile?
pool.rationale:
Conventional excimer laser ablation treats lower-order, or spherocylindrical, aberrations such as myopia, hyperopia, and astigmatism. Higher-order aberrations (HOA), such as spherical aberration, coma, and trefoil, constitute about 10% of all aberrations and cannot be treated with glasses. Some HOAs are induced by excimer laser ablation.
Wavefront-guided ablation creates ablation profiles that are customized for each individual patient to reduce preexisting higher-order aberration and minimize the induction of new aberration.
Wavefront-optimized ablation does not use patient-specific data. Instead, it adjusts a conventional ablation pattern to reduce spherical aberration. However, it has no effect on other HOAs.
Wavefront-guided ablation appears to only have clear-cut benefits over wavefront-optimized ablation in patients with significant HOAs. It is not suitable for all patients.

pool.q: What refractive surgery places a patient at highest risk for a ruptured globe from blunt trauma?

options.a: clear lens extraction with clear corneal incision
options.c: clear lens extraction with scleral corneal incision

pool.rationale: RK incisions weaken the structure of the eye for years after the procedure. A traumatic injury can lead to rupture of RK incisions and has been reported up to 13 years after RK. Although clear lens extractions with scleral or clear corneal incisions still create a weak point, they are not as susceptible to rupture as RK incisions. Full-thickness wounds are not created in LASIK, so there is less risk for a ruptured globe after LASIK than after RK.

pool.q: What clinical presentations would be an absolute contraindication to performing LASIK surgery?

options.a: myopic patient with keratometry readings of 39.00 diopters (D)
options.b: patient with untreated, active systemic connective tissue or autoimmune disease
options.c: patient with a predicted residual corneal bed less than 275 µm
options.d: hyperopic patient with keratometry readings of 46.00 D

pool.rationale:
Active connective tissue and autoimmune diseases are absolute contraindications to refractive surgery because these conditions can adversely affect healing. However, good results can be achieved in some patients with stable, inactive, well-controlled connective tissue and autoimmune diseases. Surgery in such patients might be considered off-label. The potential increased risk and possible off-label status should be discussed with the patient and documented in the medical record.
Keratometry readings lower than about 34.00 D and higher than about 50.00 D increase the risk of poor-quality vision after refractive surgery. A patient with low myopia who has a preoperative keratometry reading of 39.00 D would probably have a postoperative keratometry reading above 34.00 D.
A hyperopic patient with a preoperative keratometry reading of 46.00 D would very likely have a postoperative keratometry reading below 50.00 D.
Although the safe minimum residual corneal stromal bed thickness has not been definitively established, it should not be thinner than 250 µm because this increases the risk of corneal ectasia, unstable corneal curvature, and poor visual results.

pool.q: What variable affects the depth of laser ablation required to treat a given degree of myopia?

options.b: ambient humidity in the laser suite

pool.rationale: The amount of tissue removed centrally for myopic treatments using a broad beam laser is estimated by the Munnerlyn formula: Ablation Depth (µm) ≈ Degree of Myopia (D) × (Optical Zone diameter)2 (mm)/3. This formula shows that for a specified value of myopia, ablation depth increases by the square of the treated optical zone diameter. The effective change is independent of the initial corneal curvature. The density of the cornea might change the amount of tissue ablated per unit of laser energy, but it will not change the depth of ablation required to correct a specific degree of myopia. Because excimer laser irradiation is absorbed by hydrocarbons, increasing humidity in the laser suite might require increasing power delivered to the cornea to get the same effect at the corneal surface; however, this will not affect the depth of the laser ablation required to treat a specific degree of myopia.

pool.q: What feature is commonly found in patients with LASIK flap macrostriae?

options.b: Preoperative astigmatism is greater than 2 diopters.
options.d: Macrostriae involve the full thickness of the LASIK flap.

pool.rationale: Macrostriae (figure) occur when a LASIK flap is not positioned correctly or slips postoperatively. They involve the full thickness of the LASIK flap. Patients typically have loss of best-corrected visual acuity, and the macrostriae do not typically resolve on their own. For these reasons, prompt intervention is necessary. If the striae are significant enough to expose the intervening space between the edge of the flap and the adjacent stroma (gutter), then epithelial ingrowth can occur.

pool.q: A patient has a refractive error of -0.50 + 1.00 x 90. What pattern of incisional keratotomy would be useful to correct this refractive error?

options.a: arcuate incisions of 45 degree length at a 9 mm optical zone at the 90 and 270 degree meridians
options.b: radial incisions of 4 mm length at a 3 mm optical zone at the 90 and 270 degree meridians
options.c: arcuate incisions of 45 degree length at a 9 mm optical zone at the 180 and 360 degree meridians
options.d: radial incisions of 4 mm length at a 3 mm optical zone at the 180 and 360 degree meridians

pool.rationale: Astigmatic keratotomy is a useful technique to reduce astigmatic refractive errors. Typically, an optical zone of 7 mm to 11 mm is used. Radial incisions have been used in the past for myopic corrections, but cause a hyperopic shift, and would not be used in the refractive error in this example. The incisions at 180 and 360 degree meridians would increase the refractive error.

pool.q: A patient presents with nuclear cataracts in both eyes. He has a history of a bilateral 16-incision RK procedure with a 3-mm optical zone. His vision is limited to 20/60 best distance vision in both eyes related to the cataracts, and he undergoes cataract surgery and IOL implantation. At his 2-week postoperative visit, his vision is corrected to 20/25+ with a measured refractive error of +1.50 –0.50 × 120. He is very unhappy with his uncorrected vision, as he had hoped for either an emmetropic or a slight myopic outcome. What would be his best option for improvement?

options.a: Inform him that this is a typical outcome in RK eyes and that glasses are the best option.
options.b: Assure him that the hyperopia might lessen with resolution of corneal edema.
options.c: Plan surface ablation to correct his hyperopic outcome.
options.d: Perform an IOL exchange, leaving him hyperopic.

pool.rationale: Following cataract surgery performed on eyes that have had prior RK surgery, short-term flattening of the cornea and hyperopic shift are frequently observed, due to the corneal edema common after surgery. For this reason and in the event of a refractive surprise, neither an IOL exchange nor PRK should be considered in post-RK eyes until the cornea and refraction stabilize, which can take several weeks to months.

pool.q: In laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), a residual corneal stromal thickness of less than 250 microns is associated with what postoperative complication?
pool.rationale:
While exact mechanisms of postrefractive corneal ectasia are not fully known, a residual stromal bed thickness of less than 250 microns is a recognized risk factor for this postoperative complication. Flap creation thicker than anticipated, preoperative forme fruste keratoconus, higher myopic correction, thin corneas, and multiple laser ablations are also risk factors. However, no one risk factor is an absolute predictor of postrefractive corneal ectasia.
In order to reduce some of the risks of developing ectasia after LASIK, surgeons should review topography prior to surgery, and intraoperative pachymetry should be used to measure flap thickness and calculate the residual stromal bed after ablation to confirm whether it is safe to proceed with ablation. Treatments include collagen cross-linking and rigid gas-permeable contact lens correction. While the other 3 answer choices (epithelial ingrowth, diffuse lamellar keratitis, haze) are complications of LASIK, none are related to the residual stromal bed thickness and can occur at any residual stromal bed thickness.

pool.q: A patient presents for evaluation of laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). Her ocular history reveals a history of herpes simplex (HSV) keratitis several years ago with no recurrence. Examination reveals no cornea vascularization or thinning. What treatment is recommended for this patient?

options.a: Prescribe glasses, because the risk of virus reactivation after excimer treatment is too great, making  LASIK contraindicated.
options.b: Treat prophylactically with oral antiviral drugs prior to treatment with LASIK.
options.c: Treat with surface ablation only so that corneal sensitivity will not be reduced.
options.d: Treat prophylactically with topical corticosteroids, then if there is no recurrence of HSV, proceed with LASIK.

pool.rationale:
Refractive surgery may result in reactivation of herpesvirus, although current evidence is insufficient to determine conclusively whether surface ablation or LASIK increase the risk of recurrence in a patient with prior herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis. HSV corneal reactivation may lead to corneal ulceration, corneal thinning from stromal loss, corneal scarring, corneal vascularization, corneal neuropathy, and/or corneal edema. Corneal sensitivity may reasonably be expected decrease after refractive surgery, herpesvirus infection, or both. Oral antivirals would be indicated as a treatment for HSV keratitis and should be strongly considered as prophylaxis in these patients.
Many surgeons avoid laser vision correction in patients with a history of HSV keratitis because of concern for virus reactivation. Some surgeons will consider LASIK in a patient with a history of HSV keratitis who has not had any recurrences and who has good corneal sensation, minimal or no corneal vascularization or scarring, and excellent best-corrected visual acuity. Preoperative and postoperative prophylaxis with an oral antiviral agent should be considered strongly. Any patient with a history of herpes simplex or zoster keratitis must be counseled about the continued risk of recurrence and its concomitant potential for vision loss after excimer laser vision correction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What corneal ablation pattern has been used for the treatment of presbyopia?

options.c: a central flat zone ablation pattern

pool.rationale: Attempts to correct both distance and near vision have encompassed a variety of multifocal approaches on the cornea using the excimer laser. These approaches include using a small central steep zone, where the central portion of the cornea is for near and the midperiphery is for distance. It is not possible, though, to achieve intermediate and distance out of the same region of the cornea. Another pattern is the inferior near-zone ablation pattern. Some patterns have used an inferiorly decentered hyperopic ablation. Another pattern is a central distance with near mid-peripheral ablation. The potential issue with any of these patterns is the glare and halo experienced with reduction of contrast sensitivity.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For the depicted post-LASIK epithelial ingrowth (arrows), what clinical feature indicates that observation is appropriate?
pool.rationale: Epithelial ingrowth occurs in fewer than 3% of LASIK cases. In most cases, epithelial ingrowth appears as peripheral, isolated nests of cells that are benign and mild enough to warrant observation. More severe cases present with a decrease in visual acuity, which is usually from irregular astigmatism, flap melting, or progression toward the visual axis. These situations require treatment. Any staining at the edge of the flap indicates a fistula with active inward migration of epithelial cells, which also warrants treatment. Treatment consists of lifting the flap and removing epithelial cells from the stromal bed, underside of the flap, and peripheral cornea. The flap is then repositioned and a bandage contact lens is placed. Recurrent cases may also require flap suturing or fibrin glue.

pool.q: What change in an arcuate keratotomy procedure might result in overcorrection?

options.a: incision placed at a larger optical zone
options.c: incision placed at a smaller optical zone

pool.rationale: For an arcuate keratotomy procedure, cylindrical correction can be increased by increasing the length or depth of the incision, using multiple incisions or reducing the optical zone.

pool.q: What is the appropriate treatment for a sterile infiltrate after photorefractive keratectomy (PRK)?

options.b: continued use of a bandage contact lens
options.d: continued use of topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)

pool.rationale: Sterile infiltrates, which have been reported in 1 in 300 cases, may occur after surface ablation and are associated with the use of contact lenses to aid in epithelial healing, especially in patients using topical NSAIDs for longer than 24 hours without concomitant topical corticosteroids. They are secondary to an immune reaction, and corticosteroid administration is indicated, in addition to the tapering and cessation of topical NSAIDs and of bandage contact lens use. Close follow-up is indicated. Because any corneal infiltrate may be infectious in origin, careful consideration of a corneal infection, including a careful examination and history, is indicated prior to any treatment for a sterile infiltrate. If an infection is suspected, diagnostic corneal scraping and culture are indicated.

pool.q: How does conductive keratoplasty affect the cornea?

options.a: It works by increasing the curvature of the central cornea.
options.b: The effect is mediated by a holmium: yttrium-aluminum-garnet laser.
options.c: It works by decreasing the curvature of the central cornea.
options.d: It results in a permanent change in the shape of the cornea.

pool.rationale: Conductive keratoplasty (CK) works by radiofrequency shrinking of collagen lamellae in the cornea. It has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of hyperopia and presbyopia. The CK probe is applied at various intervals in the periphery of the cornea. A small corneal scar is initially seen, which fades over time. The peripheral shrinking of the corneal collagen (figure) results in an increase in the curvature of the central cornea. The holmium: yttrium-aluminum-garnet laser has been used in laser thermokeratoplasty, which CK has replaced. One disadvantage of CK is that the effects are often temporary.

pool.q: What is a risk factor for the creation of a buttonhole during laser In situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?
pool.rationale: Buttonhole flaps or thin flaps are more likely to be created when the cornea is very steep, typically greater than 48 diopters. Free caps are more likely to be created when the cornea is very flat, typically less than 40 diopters. Epithelial sloughing and epithelial ingrowth are more likely to result from refractive surgery when the cornea has evidence of epithelial basement membrane dystrophy. Enhancements should be assessed for Ks that are safe for refractive surgery based on the above parameters but are at no more risk for a buttonhole flap than a cornea with the same keratometric power.

pool.q: Conductive keratoplasty is a collagen shrinkage procedure approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for what refractive condition?

options.b: early treatment of post-LASIK (laser in situ keratomileusis) corneal ectasia
options.d: treatment of progressive hyperopia after radial keratotomy (RK)

pool.rationale: Conductive keratoplasty was studied in FDA clinical trials for presbyopia and approved for this indication. However, long-term follow-up of CK patients reveals inadequate and/or lack of adequate effect with the procedure. It is not FDA approved for corneal ectasia, keratoconus, or radial keratotomy (RK) patients, or in patients with post-keratoplasty astigmatism.

pool.q: According to US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidelines, what is the upper limit for myopic and astigmatic error indicated for the use of orthokeratology?

options.a: -6.00 D of myopia and 1.75 D of astigmatism
options.b: -3.00 D of myopia and 2.50 D of astigmatism
options.c: -3.00 D of myopia and 1.75 D of astigmatism
options.d: -6.00 D of myopia and 2.50 D of astigmatism

pool.rationale: Orthokeratology is indicated for the temporary reduction of myopia up to 6.00 diopters (D) in nondiseased eyes with astigmatism up to 1.75 D. It is not approved for higher myopia, higher astigmatism, or hyperopia.

pool.q: For a patient with a free cap after attempted cutting of a LASIK flap, what treatment would you recommend?

options.a: Discard the corneal cap and proceed with treatment.
options.b: Discard the cap and proceed with PRK at a later date when the epithelium has healed.
options.c: Place the corneal cap in a moist chamber and proceed with treatment if the stromal bed is large enough.
options.d: Replace the cap and proceed with photorefractive keratectomy (PRK).

pool.rationale: Free corneal caps seem to be associated with relatively flat corneas. Assuming the stromal bed is large enough to allow for treatment, it is safe to proceed with ablation. The cap should be placed in a moist chamber to prevent dehydration and replaced at the end of the treatment. A bandage contact lens should be placed until the endothelial pump can secure the cap. Discarding the cap can result in significant stromal scarring and is not appropriate in this case. Replacing the cap and proceeding with photorefractive keratectomy is inappropriate as it can result in unpredictable refractive and corneal scarring outcomes.

pool.q: After laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), what is the best management of epithelial ingrowth associated with flap melting?
pool.rationale: If the epithelial ingrowth leads to melting of the flap, the epithelium should be debrided. Observation would lead to worsening of the ingrowth and melting. Topical corticosteroids and topical mitomycin are not indicated in the treatment of epithelial ingrowth.

pool.q: What condition is a contraindication for performing laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?

options.b: myopia with flat keratometry of 39.25 diopters
options.d: residual corneal bed less than 250 µm

pool.rationale:
Several ocular and systemic conditions represent relative contraindications to refractive surgery. Although there is no absolute value that ensures corneal ectasia after refractive surgery will not occur, a residual stromal bed of 250 µm has been suggested and generally considered an acceptable minimum.
While uncontrolled collagen vascular disease is an absolute contraindication, multiple studies have reported on the safety of laser vision correction in patients with stable, well-controlled connective tissue disease. All patients with stable collagen vascular disease should be counseled about the risks of corneal thinning, keratolysis, irregular healing, and keratitis.
Excessively steep or flat corneas are a relative but not absolute contraindication to LASIK; corneas flatter than 40.0 D are at risk for transection of the hinge and creation of a free flap. Keloid formation, listed as a warning (in photorefractive keratectomy [PRK]) or precaution (in LASIK) by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the possibility of corneal scarring, is no longer considered a contraindication to laser vision correction, because several studies have demonstrated good results without significant scarring.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Six weeks after bilateral LASIK surgery that was associated with early inflammation and a prolonged steroid treatment course because of that inflammation, the patient reports several days of decreased vision in the right eye. The right eye best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) is 20/40 -2, the conjunctiva is not injected, the flap interface has diffuse haze and a prominent interface region with apparent cystic space, and the intraocular pressure (IOP) is 19 mm Hg by applanation of the central cornea. What is the most likely explanation for the patient's current symptoms?
pool.rationale:
In a small number of LASIK patients, fluid can accumulate in the flap interface due to elevated IOP, resulting in a condition that resembles DLK. This is known as pressure-induced stromal keratopathy (PISK). It is believed to result from transudation of aqueous across the stromal bed, resulting from steroid-induced elevated IOP. Fluid collected in the potential space between the flap and bed causes erroneous applanation tonometry readings that are lower than the intraocular pressure, since they represent the pressure in the interface space. Post-LASIK steroid response associated with interface fluid can be differentiated from DLK. Typically, DLK is seen from postoperative day 1 to 3 and resolves by day 7 to 10. A patient who has been on topical steroids for treatment of DLK and has not had resolution in 10 days, or has been considered for a new diagnosis of DLK after postoperative day 10, should be carefully evaluated for interface fluid. DLK has an earlier onset and is responsive to steroids, whereas interface fluid from elevated IOP typically occurs later and is unresponsive to steroids. IOP in these cases should be measured peripherally and using other methods such as Tono-Pen or pneumotonometry.
In addition to the presence of fluid in the interface, clues that suggest elevated IOP include central steepening and peripheral microcystic edema and haze. Flap dehiscence often is associated with a history or trauma and is obvious on clinical examination. Microbial keratitis can be distinguished by the presence of infiltrate that extends beyond the flap border and associated anterior chamber reaction and anterior segment (conjunctival) inflammation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Prior to refractive surgery, how long should patients be advised to avoid use of rigid contact lenses?
pool.rationale: Contact lens wear can result in corneal warpage. Many surgeons recommend that patients discontinue use of soft contact lenses for 3 days to 2 weeks, soft toric contact lenses for 2 weeks or longer, and rigid contact lenses for 2–3 weeks prior to refractive surgery evaluation. This allows the cornea to resume its normal, baseline characteristics, which can then be used to plan refractive surgery and avoid surprises due to corneal distortion or warp. For some long-term hard contact lens wearers, the cornea might require months to return to a stable curvature, and sequential corneal mapping is recommended to document stability.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: One week after cataract surgery with toric intraocular lens (IOL) implantation, a patient has an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/50 in the operated eye and a normal slit-lamp examination. The best-corrected visual acuity is 20/20 with a refraction of +0.50 -2.00 × 30. What should the ophthalmologist initially do to further understand the patient's impaired vision?

options.a: observation to allow postoperative edema to resolve
options.b: dilation to assess the toric IOL's axis
options.c: dilation to assess cystoid macular edema
options.d: corneal topography to assess corneal ectasia

pool.rationale: Persistent astigmatism after cataract surgery with toric IOL implantation is most likely due to rotation of the IOL. These patients should be dilated to verify the axis of the toric IOL. If the axis has shifted, then surgical intervention may be necessary to reposition the IOL. For the patient described, corneal ectasia is unlikely, and cystoid macular edema would not induce astigmatism. Further observation to allow corneal edema to resolve is unnecessary, because the best-corrected visual acuity is 20/20.

pool.q: A 35-year-old patient with a refraction of -8.25 D sphere in both eyes desires ocular refractive surgery. What refractive surgery procedure poses the highest risk of retinal detachment?
pool.rationale: Many refractive surgery candidates have high myopia, which independently places them at higher risk for retinal tears and detachments. Of the existing refractive surgical procedures, refractive lens exchange (RLE), is an intraocular procedure with identical risks to cataract surgery, and thus the highest risk of postoperative retinal detachment. Phakic intraocular lens placement is also an intraocular refractive procedure, but has a lower risk of retinal detachment, as there is minimal vitreous destabilization, and the crystalline lens is undisturbed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Refractive Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents 8 months after penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) with the complaint of poor vision due to astigmatism. The patient is interested in laser refractive surgery. What is recommended for the patient?

options.a: Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) is the best option, because creation of a laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) flap risks dehiscence of the transplant.
options.b: The patient should wait at least one year after PKP, and the refraction should be stable.
options.c: LASIK is the best option to avoid postoperative haze induced by PRK.
options.d: Due to the risk of graft dehiscence and the unpredictable nature of the results, laser refractive surgery should be avoided in patients who have undergone PKP.

pool.rationale:
Laser refractive surgery is an option for improving refractive error after penetrating keratoplasty (PKP). Most surgeons advocate waiting at least 1 year after transplant and an additional 4 months after sutures are removed. Additionally, refraction and corneal topography should be stable by measuring on multiple visits at least 1 month apart.

Both LASIK and PRK are options for patients who are post-PKP. To avoid postoperative haze associated with PRK, mitomycin C should be used. LASIK after PKP is subject to the same patient evaluation constraints as conventional LASIK. There is a small but significant risk of wound dehiscence during both LASIK and PRK; therefore, the graft-host interface must be carefully inspected for areas of variable coaptation.
Although the results of laser refractive surgery in post-PKP eyes are less accurate and predictable than in eyes with naturally occurring refractive errors, the surgery can still significantly reduce refractive error and improve the visual outcome when combined with glasses or contact lenses.

pool.q: A 45-year-old woman has a persistent central corneal epithelial defect 2 weeks after photorefractive keratectomy. What class of oral medication might be helpful in improving wound healing?
pool.rationale:
Persistent epithelial defects after surface ablation are common in keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and connective tissue diseases and autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis are associated with dry eye states. Diabetes mellitus and current smokers can also have poor epithelial healing.

Treatment options include aggressive nonpreserved lubrication, topical cyclosporine (a calcineurin inhibitor), temporary punctal occlusion, amniotic membrane grafting, and autologous serum drops. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) should be discontinued in patients with delayed reepithelialization. Nonpreserved drops are preferable.

Oral tetracycline-family antibiotics can be beneficial for persistent epithelial defects because they inhibit collagenase activity and in turn improve wound healing. None of the other answer choices are typically used orally to treat delayed reepithelialization.

pool.q: Coma contributes to what type of refractive abnormality?
pool.rationale:
Wavefront aberrations, representing total aberration of the entire visual system, are most commonly specified by Zernike polynomials that describe surfaces. The most important Zernike coefficients affecting visual quality are coma, spherical aberration, and trefoil. These are all higher-order aberrations and increase as a function of pupil size and age. Higher-order aberrations  result from surface shape abnormalities that are not well-corrected by spectacles or soft contact lenses. Coma produces an irregular image with vertical and horizontal blur and results when rays at one edge of the pupil come into focus before rays at the opposite edge. Coma can be seen in decentered penetrating keratoplasty grafts, keratoconus, and decentered refractive ablations.
Myopia, hyperopia, and regular astigmatism requiring spherical and/or cylindrical correction are all lower-order aberrations. Typically, these can be corrected by spectacles and include positive defocus (produced by myopia) and negative defocus (produced by hyperopia).
Conventional nonwavefront-guided excimer laser ablations typically increase higher-order aberrations, but wavefront-optimized and wavefront-guided ablations tend to induce fewer higher-order aberrations. Rigid gas-permeable (RGP) contact lenses are an effective treatment for irregular astigmatism.

pool.q: What complication of limbal relaxing incisions can be avoided with the use of a toric intraocular lens implant for correction of regular astigmatism during cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: Limbal relaxing incisions (LRI) or astigmatic keratotomy (AK) can be performed to treat regular astigmatism in a variety of settings, including cataract surgery. A patient with regular astigmatism would be a candidate for placement of peripheral corneal incisions or a toric intraocular lens implant to reduce spectacle dependence after surgery. Corneal perforation is a complication that is unique to LRI and AK, and thus is the correct answer choice in this stem. Both LRI/AK and toric lens implants can be placed in an incorrect axis and thus it is important that appropriate reference marks be placed with the patient seated upright and looking at a distance target prior to surgery. Lens implant rotation is a complication unique to toric lenses and not corneal incisions. Additionally, the worsening of astigmatism is a potential complication of both methods for correcting astigmatic error.

pool.q: A myopic patient (-8.50 OU) has LASIK that changes his distance refractive error to plano OU. For what condition does he remain at increased risk?
pool.rationale: Whether excimer laser refractive surgery is performed or not, patients with highly myopic eyes remain at risk for retinal tears and detachments. Performing photorefractive keratectomy or LASIK that eliminates their myopia does not reduce this risk. These patients are not at an increased risk for early cataract formation or developing dry eyes. In the absence of any other risk factors, this patient is not at increased risk of ectasia, either.

pool.q: Following cataract surgery, a surgeon realizes that his patient had prior laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) for high myopia. Manual keratometry values were used in the intraocular lens (IOL) calculation. What is the most likely refractive outcome and why?

options.a: The patient is myopic; the measured K value underestimated the true corneal power.
options.b: The patient is myopic; the measured K value overestimated the true corneal power.
options.c: The patient is hyperopic; the measured K value overestimated the true corneal power.
options.d: The patient is hyperopic; the measured K value underestimated the true corneal power.

pool.rationale:
Determining the keratometric power after refractive surgery for calculating IOL power for cataract surgery is problematic. Despite a surgeon's best efforts, refractive surprises are still possible, and patients should be advised preoperatively that additional surgery, such as surface ablation, LASIK, IOL exchange, or a piggyback IOL, may be required to attain a better refractive result.
In general, difficulties in determining accurate keratometric power on a postrefractive cornea arise from a small effective central optical zone; keratometers and Placido disk-based corneal topographers typically measure the corneal curvature several millimeters away from the center. If standard keratometry readings are used to calculate IOL power in a previously myopic patient, a hyperopic postoperative refraction results because the keratometry readings are greater than the true corneal power in the central optical zone. An altered relationship between the anterior and posterior corneal curvature may also contribute to this phenomenon.
Although no method is unimpeachable, several have been developed to better estimate the central corneal power after refractive surgery, including the clinical history method, and the ASCRS Online Post-Refractive IOL Power Calculator, which uses a variety of formulas and data to assist the surgeon.

pool.q: What best characterizes the excimer laser effect on the cornea during laser refractive surgery to correct myopia?

options.a: flattening of the central cornea to increase refractive power
options.b: flattening of the central cornea to decrease refractive power
options.c: steepening of the central cornea to increase refractive power
options.d: steepening of the central cornea to decrease refractive power

pool.rationale: Treatment of myopia is done by flattening the central cornea to decrease refractive power. Steepening the central cornea to increase its refractive power is the goal in a hyperopic treatment.

pool.q: How does orthokeratology temporarily reduce myopia?

options.a: bifocal add in contact that reduces accommodative demand
options.c: overnight rigid-contact lenses fit with base curve flatter than corneal keratometry
options.d: reduced peripheral overminus in structure of contact

pool.rationale: Orthokeratology temporarily reduces myopia though the use of overnight rigid-contact lenses fit with base curve flatter than corneal keratometry. The contact lenses are used to flatten the cornea. Appropriate patients include those with low myopia, minimal to no astigmatism, and highly motivated patients. Complications are related to use of overnight contact lenses and can include punctate keratopathy, corneal epithelial defects, recurrent erosions, corneal edema, temporary or permanent induced astigmatism, and microbial ulcers.

pool.q: After refractive surgery, a patient on topical steroids presents with normal intraocular pressure (IOP), but his optic nerve looks suspicious for glaucoma and a visual field shows new defects. What would explain the patient's presentation and findings?

options.a: inaccurately low measurements of IOP resulting from reduced corneal thickness
options.b: artificial visual field abnormalities induced by spherical aberrations after refractive surgery
options.c: increased sensitivity to steroids as a result of refractive surgery
options.d: decreased clarity of the view of the optic nerve after refractive surgery

pool.rationale: Decreasing the thickness of the cornea with refractive surgery can result in an artificially low IOP, as measured with Goldmann applanation tonometry. Spherical aberrations would not cause visual field defects. The clarity of the view of the optic nerve should not be affected by refractive surgery. Fluid accumulation in the interface could also result in an incorrectly measured low IOP. The sensitivity to steroids is not changed by refractive surgery.

pool.q: For a patient with a persistent epithelial defect following photorefractive keratectomy, what treatment would you recommend?
pool.rationale: A frequent cause of delayed re-epithelialization after PRK is dry eye. Hence, appropriate treatment for these patients includes lubrication with artificial tears or ointments, or cyclosporine drops, and/or punctal occlusion. A bandage contact lens or patching may also help. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and topical anesthetic drops can result in a corneal melting, especially in someone whose corneal epithelium is not intact. Therefore, they are not part of the treatment in this patient. Phototherapeutic keratectomy would not help with treatment of a persistent epithelial defect. Patients with diabetes, patients who smoke, or patients with an undiagnosed connective tissue disease may also have delayed healing.

pool.q: Corneal transplantation may be required after refractive surgery.  What prior refractive surgery might require a larger transplant and additional sutures into the area of prior surgery?
pool.rationale: Corneal transplantation is occasionally required after refractive surgery for indications including significant scarring, irregular astigmatism, ectasia, and edema. Issues unrelated to refractive surgery, such as trauma, infectious keratitis, or corneal edema after cataract surgery, can also necessitate corneal transplantation. After RK, peripheral incisions may gape or dehisce during penetrating keratoplasty, and even though a larger graft may be used, the additional measure of placing sutures into the peripheral incisions to reduce wound gape may be required. In LASIK and intracorneal ring segment patients, a larger graft may be required to get around the peripheral area of the flap or segments, but typically, additional sutures into the area of the flap or channels are not required. In patients with ectasia, an analysis of where the tissue is ectatic should be undertaken to improve the astigmatic results by not leaving areas of ectatic tissue.

pool.q: What is the most concerning complication of epithelial ingrowth after laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?
pool.rationale:
Epithelial ingrowth occurs more commonly in patients having LASIK when epithelial basement membrane dystrophy is present preoperatively, with flap trauma or with flap lift enhancements. The epithelium under the flap prevents nutrition of the flap, leading to melting of the flap.
Ectasia and DLK are not related to epithelial ingrowth. Infectious keratitis does not typically lead to or result from epithelial ingrowth.

pool.q: A patient undergoes uncomplicated laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) for high myopia. At 1 week, the patient sees 20/20 in each eye uncorrected, but regression occurs, and 4 months after surgery the patient undergoes an enhancement for residual myopia. Six months after the enhancement, the patient complains of blurred vision. Acuity measures 20/40 in each eye. Refraction fluctuates during exam, but -1.25 + 1.00 × 52 OD and -1.50 + 0.75 × 30 OS can achieve 20/25 acuity in each eye. Slit-lamp exam reveals a clear cornea and healthy flap. No posterior pathology is present. What is the best next step?
pool.rationale: A best corrected vision of 20/25 in a patient who previously saw 20/20 needs to be evaluated. A topography would help in the evaluation of potential ectasia. Patients who need an enhancement are at higher risk for developing ectasia. An enhancement would potentially worsen the ectasia and should not be performed without knowing the reason for decreased acuity. Glasses are unlikely to satisfy the patient because this is not a good or expected result.

pool.q: Six months after refractive surgery, a patient has a visually significant central island. He wants additional laser treatment to treat this problem. What counselling should he be given about the treatment options for central islands?

options.a: An unpredictable outcome is more likely with topography-guided laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK).
options.b: The occurrence of central islands is more likely with the use of variable-spot-size lasers.
options.c: With observation most central islands diminish over time, although resolution may take 6-12 months.
options.d: Haze formation is less likely with surface ablation retreatment.

pool.rationale: A central island is defined as a steepening of at least 1.00 D with a diameter of less than 1 mm, compared with the paracentral flattened area. Central islands may be associated with decreased visual acuity, monocular diplopia and multiplopia, ghost images, and decreased contrast sensitivity. Central islands are becoming less common with use of variable spot size lasers. Most central islands diminish over time, especially after surface ablation, although resolution may take 6-12 months. The treatment outcomes are unpredictable no matter what approach is used; however, options such as topography-guided ablations may be helpful in treating persistent central islands. Haze formation is a risk of surface ablation.

pool.q: In the Helmholtz theory, what happens to achieve accommodation?
pool.rationale: In the Helmholtz theory, the lens increases in dioptric power and “rounds up” at the anterior and posterior surfaces because when the ciliary muscles contract, all zonules relax. The lens diameter decreases and the pupil constricts during accommodation. In the Schachar theory of accommodation, ciliary contraction and an increase in equatorial zonular tension results in increased lens curvature. In that theory, presbyopia occurs because the increase in lens diameter reduces increases in equatorial zonular tension, and anything that increases resting equatorial zonular tension, such as scleral expansion, should restore accommodation.

pool.q: Following manifest refraction, a patient has a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/40. She wants LASIK to improve her distance vision. Given her topography as shown, what counsel should the ophthalmologist give her?

options.a: She is a candidate for photorefractive keratectomy (PRK).
options.b: She is a candidate for LASIK.
options.c: She is not a candidate for ablative refractive surgery.
options.d: She should be re-examined in 2 to 3 months and, if the topography is stable, LASIK or PRK can be performed.

pool.rationale: This patient has corneal topography that shows inferior steepening that is most consistent with keratoconus (KCN). KCN is generally considered a contraindication to refractive surgery, as ablation of the corneal stroma may result in further loss of structural integrity and worsening ectasia. Topography is important in the preoperative evaluation of refractive surgery, as it may aid in the detection of early KCN. Indeed, asymmetric inferior corneal steepening or asymmetric bow-tie topography are well-established risk factors for progression to KCN and post-LASIK ectasia. Serial topography is not necessary, as one would not expect this to improve by observation; it would be more appropriate in a patient with contact lens wear and topography suspicious for contact-lens-induced corneal warpage, as this can reverse.
